articles.title: Watch: Moment sneaker shop in Indonesia is torn apart by explosion
articles.summary: Police have said it is “strongly suspected” that the incident was caused by a gas leak.
articles.body:
CCTV has captured the moment a sneaker shop was torn apart by an explosion in the San Antonio area of Surabaya, Indonesian authorities have confirmed.

Police have said five people have been hospitalised following the incident that was “strongly suspected” to be the result of a gas leak, and no suspicious substances or explosives have been found at the site.

They added that at least 41 buildings had been damaged by the explosion.

articles.title: I was 16 when I started reselling online. A few months later, my garage was a warehouse and I was making $25,000 a month.
articles.summary: Ethan Alexander started reselling Walmart products on Amazon as a teenager. His family's garage soon became a makeshift warehouse.
articles.body:
Ethan Alexander was a high school sophomore when he started reselling goods on Amazon.

He did $125,000 in sales last year, before the business became overwhelming.

He's invested much of the money and plans to use what he learned from the business.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ethan Alexander . It has been edited for length and clarity .

Each year, I get a $500 gift from an investment account that my great-grandfather set up for all of his great-grandkids. My gramps — Jack Davis — owned his own company and left a legacy of entrepreneurship in our family.

I get the money on his birthday, May 9th. In 2025, my sophomore year of high school, I came across a video on Instagram about making a profit by reselling items online shortly after I received Gramp's gift. I had stopped playing lacrosse, my typical spring sport, and I was looking for something to fill my time. I used the $500 to pay someone to teach me how to resell.

I didn't do much research, just thought "what's the worst that can happen?" The business took off immediately, and I generated just under $10,000 in revenue that first month. In August, I did more than $25,000 in revenue.

I resold lots of goods at a relatively small profit

Success reselling on Amazon comes from volume. I would find a product where I could make a relatively small profit margin — about $2 to $4 — and sell lots of it. To find these products, I utilized software that many Amazon sellers use. I also used AI to create my own system for finding products.

The first product I sold was laundry detergent , which I could buy at Walmart and resell on Amazon for about a 25% profit. I'd spend hours driving my truck to all the Walmarts in Greater Kansas City, buying as much detergent as I could fit. The garage at my home looked like a warehouse.

After spending afternoons buying the goods, I'd stay up until the early morning packaging them. Then, I'd wake up in the early afternoon and bring my shipments to the post office. Before long, they knew me by name.

I learned about the rewards of business and the risks

The work wasn't glamorous. I was essentially working a warehouse job in my own house. I didn't see much of my friends that summer, because I was focused on scaling my sales.

My mom was a huge asset. She runs her own health and wellness business and is also a business coach. I'm always willing to learn, so I listened to what she told me, and also drew on the skills you learn growing up in an entrepreneurial family.

Still, there were lots of little challenges. I was a minor, and some months I was making $45,000 in purchases. At first, I used my mom's credit card for those transactions, but it kept getting flagged as fraud . Eventually, I had to go to the bank and take out a large amount of cash for my Walmart runs.

I hired a few people to help me pack items, but one of them put the wrong labels on products, a mistake that cost me thousands. I learned about not mixing friendships and business that way. I also had frustrations with the backend of Amazon's seller platforms.

I was making good money and incredibly proud of what I had built — but I also learned a lot about the risks of business, not just the rewards.

I want to own my own business in the future

By February 2026, running the business became overwhelming. My grades were suffering. As a seller, I needed to keep the momentum up to get more sales, so there wasn't really a way to scale back. I decided to stop the business for now.

I spent some of the money on splurges, like clothes and Meta glasses. I've also invested a lot of it.

Now I'm 18, and entering my senior year of high school. I plan to go to college, because I don't see a reason not to — especially since my parents have a college savings account for me. I'm curious, though, whether I'll learn more in business school than I did from running my own business.

I know one thing for certain: I plan to be an entrepreneur. There's no other option, as far as I'm concerned.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

articles.title: How Adidas's Harry Miles thinks supershoes can reach every runner
articles.summary: The shoe on the table beside Harry Miles is one almost nobody reading this will ever wear.
articles.body: The shoe on the table beside Harry Miles is one almost nobody reading this will ever wear. The Adizero Sprint Spike Concept, one of many concepts Adidas had on show, is made for sprinters who run 100 metres in under 10 seconds, whose feet touch the ground for about a tenth of a second on each stride, under forces several times their body weight.Miles directs footwear innovation at Adidas and has worked on everything from custom shoes for ultramarathon record attempts to football boots, so he knows better than most how far that spike is from the way most people run."You wouldn't take this onto the road if you're doing a 5K jog in the morning," he said at Adidas's Home of Innovation in Herzogenaurach, where the company opened its labs to visitors over the Berlin Marathon weekend.That distance runs through the entire supershoe category. Since carbon-plated racers with high-rebound foams arrived in 2017, every major sportswear brand has built its fastest shoes around the same basic recipe. The word "supershoe" has done a lot of marketing work since then, but underneath it sits a fairly precise piece of engineering.That engineering peaked in April, when Sabastian Sawe ran the first official sub-two-hour marathon in Adidas's Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3, a shoe tuned for someone covering a kilometre in under 2 minutes 50 seconds. Yomif Kejelcha crossed the line 11 seconds behind him in the same shoe. On Sunday in Berlin, the Evo 3 swept both the men's and women's podiums, the first time a single brand has done that at a major marathon since 2017.The Evo 3 also points to where the category is heading. It is designed to last a single marathon, its foam and upper too fragile for much more, and it costs $500 in the US, when you can find one at all. Shoes like it are starting to be called hypershoes, a tier above the supershoes that defined the last decade.That leaves the Adizero Adios Pro 5, launched days before Berlin, as the supershoe tier below the Evo 3. It was on many feet at this year's race, and plenty more runners have had their eyes on it, and then on its eye-watering price.A runner at 6 minutes per kilometre also lands, loads and pushes off shoes like these in a very different way from Sawe. Closing that gap, Miles says, is the point of the work."The most important part of what we do is not only delivering for the few people who are capable of breaking world records, but also making sure it becomes accessible at scale for the masses."How that happens is an engineering question, and his answer starts with what a supershoe is actually for.A supershoe's sole purpose is saving energyAsk Miles what a supershoe does and he doesn't talk about speed. He talks about efficiency, and uses an electric car to explain it.A runner starts every race fully charged. The more efficient the system, the less charge it uses at any given pace, so the runner can either go faster for the same effort or reach the final kilometres with something left in the battery. For most people buying these shoes, that is a more honest pitch than speed. Very few of them will ever race anyone but themselves.Sports scientists call this running economy, the oxygen a runner needs to hold a steady pace, and measuring it is about as unglamorous as the field gets. The athlete runs, usually on a treadmill, with a mask strapped to their face while a gas analyser reads every breath. Miles describes the same routine at Adidas: prototypes on athletes' feet, masks on their faces, and the numbers deciding which version survives.Weight is where the easiest gains are. Since the 1980s, researchers have known that every 100 grams added to a shoe raises the energy cost of running by about 1 per cent, because that weight has to be lifted and swung on every stride. Run those numbers across the tens of thousands of steps in a marathon and it is easy to see why the industry has spent four decades shaving grams.The Evo 3 weighs 97 grams, with rubber cut down to a thin layer only where the foot needs grip. Adidas says it is 1.6 per cent more economical than the previous Evo, though that figure comes from the company, not independent testing.A lab session only captures an athlete on one day. The fuller picture comes from training, and this is where AI comes into shoe design.Adidas collects training data through smartwatches and sensors it gives athletes at training camps. Miles says all of it, along with the lab data, ends up in "big machine learning systems" that surface the right insights from the right athletes far faster than before.Anyone who has opened a running watch export will understand why. One session produces continuous readings of stride, ground contact time, cadence and heart rate, and across dozens of athletes and months of training, that becomes far more than any team can compare by hand. Finding patterns in more numbers than anyone has time to read is exactly the kind of job machine learning suits.Miles is careful to call it one tool among many at Adidas, and that restraint makes the claim easier to believe.The real engineering is buried in the midsoleStrip a racing shoe down and most of its efficiency sits in two parts, the foam and the carbon. These are also the parts Miles expects to reach ordinary runners first, and in Adidas's line-up, some of it already has.A midsole works like a spring. It compresses when the foot lands, stores energy and gives part of it back at push-off. Whatever it doesn't give back is lost as heat inside the material, which engineers call hysteresis.The aim is a foam that loses less energy and weighs less, and Adidas says Lightstrike Pro Evo, the foam in the Evo 3, is around half the weight of the previous version. That previous version, Lightstrike Pro, shows how the trickle-down works.The Adizero Evo SL uses that racing foam on its own, with no rods, in a simple construction, and it costs less than the plated Boston 13. Further down the range, the Adizero SL2 blends Lightstrike Pro with the older Lightstrike 2.0 EVA foam and regularly turns up in sales. Each step down trades a bit of race-day bounce for a lower price and a longer life.That longer life matters. Very light, very bouncy foams tend to wear out sooner than the denser foams in everyday trainers, which makes a supershoe closer to a consumable than a long-term buy. The hyper shoe takes that to its logical end: one race, and done. Anyone who has retired a pair of racers earlier than planned will know the feeling.Carbon's job is less obvious. At push-off, the joints where the toes meet the foot bend, and that bending absorbs energy the runner never gets back. A stiff carbon structure limits the bend and, together with a curved rocker sole, rolls the foot forward. Miles likens getting that stiffness right to picking a gear: too little and the runner is in the wrong one, too much and the gear is set too high to be quick.Brands have approached that stiffness in different ways, from full-length plates to separate carbon rods, and Adidas has just changed its own approach. The Evo 3 drops the traditional plate for a carbon Energyrim, which lets Adidas fit more foam underfoot while staying within World Athletics' limits. The Pro 5 inherits it, replacing the rod-shaped Energyrods of earlier Adios Pro models, and the company says it returns 9 per cent more energy than the previous version.The rods haven't disappeared, though. The Boston 13 borrows the Energyrods from the Adios Pro 4 to add punch to faster training sessions, and Adidas describes the ones in that shoe as glass-fibre Energyrods 2.0, tuned for a softer but still propulsive ride. They are a less rigid, less expensive version of the same idea.It's a long run from the track to the roadThis is why the spike on the table can't simply be scaled down. A sprinter's foot is on the ground so briefly that the shoe works almost entirely at the forefoot, under loads a jogger never comes close to. A recreational runner's foot stays down more than twice as long and often lands further back, so the foam stiffness, plate shape and rocker all have to be tuned again before any of the thinking carries over. Presenting the concept, Miles put the gap in numbers. Sawe took roughly 20,000 steps to win in London, while Oblique Seville won last year's 100 m world title in fewer than 50, which leaves a spike under a quarter of a per cent of the steps to make its difference.Spike technology has already crossed over once. For its F50+ football boot, Adidas took the stiff plate and lightweight, high-rebound foam from its track spikes and adapted them for footballers, a project Miles co-wrote about for the company. The Sprint Spike Concept, as it happens, borrows the Evo 3's Energyrim and Lightstrike Pro Evo foam, so the traffic already runs both ways. A road shoe is the next and harder crossing, because a jogger's stride is further from a sprinter's than a winger's is.Miles says that is the work Adidas is doing now: looking at how the principles that make a spike fast over 100 metres could become something a person out for an early 5 km on a Sunday can feel. He puts it a few years out, after which this kind of technology becomes, in his words, "more accessible and more usable" for road runners.The Pro 5 shows how that usually plays out. It carries Evo 3 technology at a price that still keeps it out of reach for many, and for most runners the benefit only arrives once it trickles down again into trainers like the Evo SL and the Boston.The hyper shoe may speed that up. Every time the ceiling moves higher, what used to sit at the top moves down a tier. The foams and carbon that defined race day a few years ago now turn up in trainers with entry-level price tags across brands, and the Evo SL is Adidas's version of that. For everyday runners, a $500 shoe that lasts one race is less a product to buy than a preview of what their next pair might carry.How quickly that happens depends on how fast the company learns. One of the slowest parts of building a shoe, Miles says, has always been the wait between testing a prototype with an athlete and having data worth acting on.At three months per prototype, a team gets about four attempts a year. At one month, it gets roughly twelve, each tested and refined before the design is locked."If you close the loop much quicker, you can learn faster," he says, sounding more like a software engineer than a shoe designer. It is also the most convincing case in the conversation for how elite technology gets fast-tracked to the rest of us.Taken far enough, that loop could close around a single foot. Almost every shoe today is built on a last, a standard foot-shaped mould, with the same foam density running through the midsole, which means it is designed for an average foot that nobody actually has.Earlier in the day at Adidas's APEX Lab, I had seen what the alternative looks like: shoes 3D printed for individual athletes. The printer is the part everyone photographs, but the more interesting work happens before it starts. A foot scan and motion capture map where an athlete's foot takes the most pressure, where it flexes and how force moves through it on every stride, and the shoe is built around that map instead of an average. Every new session sharpens the map for the next pair, which is Miles's loop at its most personal. For now, only a handful of athletes get to wear one.The weekend runner is still the hardest customer to design forThe further a runner is from that handful, the less certain the science gets. Independent research on everyday runners is still unsettled. Some studies find the economy gain narrows at slower paces, with a few runners measuring worse in the shoes, while others find it holds.Part of the problem is that there is no such thing as a typical weekend runner. An elite field sits in a narrow band of bodyweights, cadences and foot strikes, and Adidas can fit a shoe to each athlete in it. The runners behind them at a city marathon range from heel strikers to forefoot runners and from 50 kg to 100 kg, often on roads far rougher than a closed race course. They need one shoe that works for all of them, lasts hundreds of kilometres and costs a fraction of a racer. That is a harder brief than a world record.The maths does have a quirk that favours slower runners. Someone on the course for four and a half hours gains more minutes from the same percentage improvement than someone finishing in just over two, so a small efficiency gain means more to them, not less.So what does a sub-two-hour marathon change for someone running 5 km on a Sunday? Not much right away. Super shoes at the very top, or hypershoes as the likes of the Evo 3 are now being called, will stay rare and expensive. Over the next few years, though, what was learned building them will filter down, first into shoes like the Pro 5 and then into more affordable trainers such as the Adizero Evo SL, Boston and SL2. That slow trickle, more than any record, is what Miles means when he talks about reaching the masses.Whether any of it ever shows up on a recreational runner's watch is still an open question. The more likely payoff is one the watch won't record at all: a run that leaves a little more in the legs, in a shoe that carries a little of what was built for the front of the race.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Tories pledge £10bn British 'Iron Dome' air defence system
articles.summary: The Conservatives say their plan would protect the UK at a time when Nato allies have warned of Russian drone incursions.
articles.body:
The Conservatives have pledged to invest £10bn in a British "Iron Dome", inspired by Israel's elaborate air defence system, to defend the UK if they win the next general election.

The party said the so-called "Britannia Shield" would offer the UK an integrated network of radar, command and control systems, as well as interceptor missiles.

In a speech at the Tory conference on Tuesday, shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge will describe it as "the most significant upgrade to UK air defence for generations".

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Tories had an "abysmal record" of defending Britain during their 14 years in power, adding: "They owe Britain an apology, not another lecture."

The party said the air defence system would be capable of defending the UK's critical national infrastructure, military bases and sovereign territories from sophisticated threats.

It added the proposal would strengthen the UK's air defence systems at a time when Nato allies have warned they are facing repeated Russian drone incursions.

The party also cited a report from the defence committee of MPs last November which said the UK was lagging behind its European counterparts in having a plan to defend itself and overseas territories from a military attack.

The Conservative Party said its "Britannia Shield" would have three components - new advanced radar systems, upgraded command and control systems to integrate information from across Britain's defences and rapidly decide a response, and new interceptor missiles as well as counter-drone capabilities.

The three-tiered design of the proposal is similar to the British Army's current Sky Sabre air defence system.

This system - which can intercept munitions and aircraft as well as integrate with wider air defences - was deployed by the UK to the Middle East earlier this year for defensive action against Iranian attacks.

In his speech at the conference in Birmingham, Cartlidge will say: "With a £10bn budget, this would be one of Britain's most significant military programmes since the cold war.

"But one that is totally necessary because of the threats we face."

Streeting said in response: "They [the Conservatives] cut the Army to its smallest size since Napoleon and left a £17 billion hole in the equipment plan.

"Their own defence secretary, Ben Wallace, admitted our Armed Forces had been 'hollowed out and underfunded'."

The Conservatives said their plan would be funded within their existing commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, paid for by welfare reform and reprioritisation of existing expenditure.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been under pressure to set out how he will reach Nato's 3.5% of GDP spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.

The current Labour government's Defence Investment Plan includes more than £350m to double the number of Sky Sabre systems operated by the British Army, with ground-based air defence sitting alongside air and maritime capabilities.

articles.summary: A convicted child rapist allegedly attacked a woman at a Planet Fitness before sexually assaulting an employee who intervened. He is being held without bail.
articles.body: A convicted child rapist allegedly attacked a woman after bringing her to a Planet Fitness gym to use the showers, then allegedly sexually assaulted an employee who tried to intervene. Laquan Holland, 40, allegedly beat the woman, tried to strip off her clothing and blocked her escape inside the Cambridge, Massachusetts, gym, the Middlesex District Attorney’s Office told Fox News Digital. The attack came weeks after a charge accusing Holland of failing to register as a sex offender was dismissed on the condition that he complete his registration, prosecutors confirmed. Holland was ordered held without bail after his arraignment on two counts of assault to rape, two counts of indecent assault and battery, kidnapping and witness intimidation. Prosecutors said Holland, a member of the Porter Square gym, arrived around 9 a.m. Oct. 1 with a woman he knew after offering to let her use the showers. But once they arrived, Holland allegedly began hitting her. CALIFORNIA DEMS TRIGGER OUTRAGE AFTER SIDING WITH CONVICTED CHILD SEX OFFENDERS IN SHOCKING VOTE The woman fled into the women’s locker room and shower area, authorities said. Holland allegedly followed, continuing to hit and touch her inappropriately while trying to remove her clothing and preventing her from leaving, according to the DA’s office. WASHINGTON MOTHER SAYS SHE FOUND ADULT MALE SHOWERING IN WOMEN'S LOCKER ROOM DURING CHILDREN'S SWIM MEET A female employee entered the shower area and tried to pull Holland off the woman. Holland’s criminal history includes guilty pleas in 2006 to two counts of child rape and one count of indecent assault and battery on a child under 14, Boston.com reported, citing court records. REPEAT OFFENDER WITH 7 PRIOR CONVICTIONS ARRESTED 3 TIMES IN 12 DAYS OVER ALLEGED ATTACKS ON WOMEN More recently, Cambridge police arrested him Aug. 25 for failing to register as a sex offender, a subsequent offense, according to police records reviewed by Fox News Digital. The DA’s office said Holland, who is homeless and was known to stay in Cambridge and Boston, must complete registration and verification requirements every 30 days. He showed up at Cambridge police headquarters to register Aug. 25 but was arrested because he was late, prosecutors said. The charge was later dismissed on the condition that he register, which he completed Aug. 27. articles.title: Chicago woman shot 5 times by Border Patrol agent files federal lawsuit
articles.summary: A Chicago woman who was shot five times by a Border Patrol agent during Operation Midway Blitz filed a lawsuit against the federal government Monday, calling...
articles.body:
CHICAGO ( WGN ) — A Chicago woman who was shot five times by a Border Patrol agent during Operation Midway Blitz filed a lawsuit against the federal government Monday, calling for more action against the agent who shot her.

Marimar Martinez said the encounter with Border Patrol agents happened in Oct. 2025. She was allegedly heading to church to drop off clothing donations when she noticed immigration officers on her street.

"For the next 15 to 20 minutes, I followed these Border Patrol agents through my neighborhood, honking my horn, shouting out 'La Migra,'" Martinez said while testifying on Capitol Hill in Feb.

Martinez said the driver of the Border Patrol vehicle she was following made eye contact with her before swerving into and hitting her truck.

"I drove forward and went around the Border Patrol agent who jumped out of his car and pointed his gun at me. I moved to the far-left lane, striking the curb on the far-left side of Kedzie (Avenue). The next thing I knew, I felt a burning sensation in my arms and legs," Martinez said. "As I continued trying to drive past the Border Patrol agents, I could hear my back passenger window shatter, and I felt bullets continue to pierce my body."

The Department of Homeland Security called her a domestic terrorist and charged her with using her vehicle to assault federal agents.

However, the Department of Justice later dropped all charges against her.

While addressing the civil lawsuit outside a downtown Chicago law office Monday, attorneys representing Martinez said they are seeking more transparency and accountability.

"We are here today, exactly one year and one day after the shooting of Marimar by agent Charles Exum. As you all know, there has been absolutely zero progress from the Department of Justice as far as accountability goes," attorney Chris Parente said. "There's been no investigation. There's been no charges."

The lawsuit alleges that Border Patrol's account of the shooting contradicts what Martinez says actually happened.

The Department of Homeland Security said that during the immigration crackdown altercation, Martinez tried to ram agents with her vehicle. Martinez maintains that she was driving away from them when one of the agents fired into her vehicle.

"What we've done here as a defense team is that we essentially became our own Department of Justice. We have hired our own experts, we have done our own investigation," Parente said.

Martinez's attorneys presented new video and photo evidence from the incident, saying it shows the agent was not in harm's way when he started shooting. Martinez said she and her family saw the material for the first time Sunday.

"It brought a lot of clarity for them. They got a lot of answers on what happened on Oct. 4," Martinez said.

Martinez said she's thankful to be alive to share her story and wants to fight for others affected by Operation Midway Blitz.

"I want to spread awareness because what's happening is not normal. We shouldn't sit here and normalize what's happening," Martinez said.

Martinez and her attorneys have been planning to sue for months.

In Feb., they filed an administrative Federal Tort Claims Act complaint, the first step in the lengthy process of filing a lawsuit against the federal government.

articles.title: Bomani Jones calls Josh Allen a "moron" for costly interception, while defending Lamar Jackson for same thing
articles.summary: Bomani Jones called Josh Allen a "moron" for his interception but cushioned Lamar Jackson's similar mistake with Hall of Fame praise and receiver blame.
articles.body: With Caitlin Clark eliminated from the remainder of the WNBA playoffs, the sports media has naturally shifted its attention to its other favorite target: Bills superstar quarterback Josh Allen. Former ESPN host Bomani Jones has spent considerable energy trying to revive his media career by manufacturing a race war between fans of Allen and Lamar Jackson. Last month, Jones accused unnamed "white folks" of favoring Allen, despite acknowledging on multiple occasions that he favors Black quarterbacks. For the record, there is no evidence that white people broadly favor Allen over Jackson. That's why Jones never gets around to naming these supposedly biased white people. Still, it's amusing to watch how determined he is to make Allen vs. Jackson a thing. And because his brand requires him to side with the Black athlete no matter the facts, he frequently invokes a senseless double standard in an attempt to justify his position. Case in point: how he covered their game-losing interceptions this season. On Monday, Jones uploaded a YouTube clip belittling Allen under the headline "Josh Allen Is Still THAT Guy…" During his critique, Jones called Allen a "moron" and suggested the Bills had made a mistake by deciding to live with his occasional recklessness. "Look, [the Bills] cast their lot on the idea that we're just gonna live with Josh Allen and whatever he does, but that's not – I don't think that's what they're talking about. Like the idea isn't and every now and then be a moron," Jones said. ESPN DESERVES CREDIT FOR PUSHING BACK ON DAN LE BATARD’S FALSE ACCUSATION OF RACISM He then mocked the idea that Allen should be the MVP favorite or considered the best quarterback in the NFL. "They still called him an MVP. We still talk that. Remember how ready everybody was to make him the best quarterback in the league and everything else. Are they still saying that now? I'm asking that." Hold that thought. Now, compare Jones' reaction to Jackson throwing a similar interception two weeks earlier in a last-second loss to the Saints. Jones acknowledged that Jackson continues to lose games late, even with a new coaching staff, but quickly cushioned the criticism by telling viewers that Jackson "is a sure-fire Hall of Famer and all of that." Then came an alternative culprit: the receiver. "I will say I felt like the way that Rashard Bateman reacted at that interception, it looked like he was the one that made the wrong move," Jones added. By the end, Jones emphasized that while Jackson struggled late, "he looked awesome, awesome for three quarters." To recap: Jackson's interception was costly, but perhaps it wasn't his fault. He's still a Hall of Famer. He was awesome for three quarters. And his receiver might actually deserve the blame. Allen throws one, and he's a "moron." There was also no sarcastic questioning of whether Jackson still belonged among the NFL's best quarterbacks, a designation Jones and his guests regularly apply to him. Subtle. DAN LE BATARD FALSELY CLAIMS THAT ESPN ONLY HIRES AND PAYS WHITE PEOPLE We first noticed this pattern in 2023, when Allen and Jackson lost in back-to-back weeks at home to the eventual Super Bowl champion Kansas City Chiefs. Jackson played considerably worse against the same defense than Allen did. He also threw another game-losing interception. Yet Jones reserved substantially more criticism for Allen. For background, Allen and Jackson are linked in the minds of the race idolaters for fairly simple reasons. They were drafted the same year and have spent most of their careers chasing Patrick Mahomes. Allen is also a white quarterback from small-town America who posted inappropriate tweets as a teenager. Jackson is a black quarterback who was overlooked by at least one anonymous scout and, according to Jemele Hill, embraces his "people" like Allen Iverson. To be clear, Jackson himself has never made his career about being black. The sports media assigned him that role. Bomani Jones is among those who insist on maintaining it. They want a rivalry between the Big Bad White Quarterback and the Disrespected Black Quarterback. It's an incredibly lazy framework, but they remain committed to it. Before the season, Jones claimed the media held Jackson to a higher standard than Allen, despite considerable evidence to the contrary. Further, the Lamar Bros. — Jones, Ryan Clark and Cam Newton among them — actually force us to diminish Jackson when they insist on comparing him to Allen. At this stage of their careers, the two quarterbacks aren't particularly close. Allen is considerably better. Don't take our word for it. Ask the people paid to evaluate NFL quarterbacks. In August, The Athletic asked 50 NFL executives and coaches to rank the league's quarterbacks entering the season. They placed Allen No. 2 in Tier 1, behind Patrick Mahomes and ahead of Matthew Stafford and Joe Burrow. Jackson ranked No. 5 — in Tier 2. A month earlier, ESPN surveyed league executives, coaches and scouts for a similar ranking. That group ranked Allen the best quarterback in football. Jackson again finished fifth, a tier below. So, whom should we trust: NFL coaches, executives and scouts, or Bomani Jones, Cam Newton and Ryan Clark? One group studies film, personnel and performance for a living. The other increasingly filters the discussion through racial narratives and the social-media reaction those narratives generate. The postseason gap is even more explicit. Take a look: Josh Allen: 38 total touchdowns, 4,682 total yards, six interceptions, a 101.4 passer rating and an 8-7 playoff record. Lamar Jackson: 13 total touchdowns, 2,394 total yards, seven interceptions, an 84.6 passer rating and a 3-5 playoff record. Just stop. Calling Allen a "moron" while treating Jackson's mistake as an invitation for contextual nuance might score culture-war points, but it doesn't create a real rivalry between the two. It's the quarterback version of Caitlin Clark vs. Angel Reese: a media rivalry sustained largely by people who desperately want the comparison to be closer than the evidence suggests. If pundits like Bomani Jones insist on pitting a White athlete against a Black athlete, they could at least wait until they find two performing at roughly the same level. Side note: Jones also tried to make Kyler Murray vs. Sam Darnold a thing this summer, after Darnold won the Super Bowl. To no one's surprise, Jones sided with Murray, the black quarterback. That one hasn't aged particularly well, either. That's the problem with racial idolatry as a substitute for analysis: eventually, the games are played. Not every moment needs to advance the race war. Sometimes a bad interception is just a bad interception.

articles.title: Nifty: Five reasons India's markets are sinking even when its economy is growing
articles.summary: The world's fastest growing major economy has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026.
articles.body:
India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-related disruptions.

But the world's fastest growing major economy also has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. The correction in Indian stocks has, in fact, only intensified in recent weeks.

The benchmark Sensex and Nifty indices, which represent the country's largest companies, have inched up slightly since Monday after posting losses for eight straight weeks - the longest losing streak in 25 years, according to Reuters.

Indian mom-and-pop investors who put their money into the Nifty have seen their wealth erode by about 15% this year. In comparison, they would have made 62% returns on Korea's Kospi index since January or 170% in the last two years.

On aggregate, the money foreign investors have put into Indian markets in the past decade - after subtracting what they sold or withdrew - is nearing zero. In the past two years alone, foreign institutional investors have withdrawn a staggering $40bn, according to data from Bernstein Research.

It is the large pool of domestic institutional and retail money, flowing into instruments like mutual funds, that have helped the markets avoid a sharper fall.

Domestic assets under management of mutual funds have grown from about $125bn in 2016 to some $900bn this year, with the number of Indians parking money in stocks and mutual funds more than tripling to 150 million individuals.

This makes the recent fall in the markets more worrying - since households, already struggling from a weak job market, high inflation and faltering consumption, are now seeing their equity savings take a beating too.

Here are five reasons India's booming economy isn't lifting its stock market.

Persistent energy shocks due to Middle East conflict

Crude oil prices have hovered between $90 and $100 a barrel as the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz enters its eighth month, far longer than analysts had expected. Moreover, there's little visibility on when normalcy will return.

"This single variable tends to influence the markets quite negatively," Hari Shyamsunder, a fund manager with Franklin Templeton Asset Management India, told the BBC. "Markets can absorb crude between $70 and $90, but when prices move above $100 a barrel, it starts putting stress on macro-economic variables such as inflation and also company earnings and margins."

India imports over 90% of its requirements - nearly half of its crude oil imports, along with a large share of its liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments, come through the Strait of Hormuz.

While Delhi has diversified its energy sources, tapping Russian oil markets, US President Donald Trump recently threatened up to 100% tariffs on countries doing trade with Moscow, further complicating matters.

With oil prices rising, inflation is going up and, as a result, interest rates are on the rise globally. The effective yield on US government bonds is above 5%, or at near 25-year highs.

These are often considered risk-free investments. As a result, foreign money tends to leave riskier emerging market assets such as Indian equities and chase safer investments like US bonds when interest rates rise.

For foreign investors, the problem of muted returns has been compounded by a weaker rupee. In currency-adjusted dollar terms, they have suffered because of the fall in the Indian currency.

The Nifty has delivered just 6% annualised dollar returns over the past decade - hardly attractive, especially in comparison with several other competing markets.

Indian stocks are cheaper, but still relatively expensive

Stock valuations have been another major concern.

The market correction over the last two years has reduced the premium that Indian stocks held over their emerging market competitors.

"Stocks are cheaper than they have been on average for the last ten years," says Shyamsunder, adding that the premium that Indian shares commanded over other emerging economies has shrunk substantially in the past few years.

However, they are still expensive relative to their earnings, especially since companies in countries such as South Korea and Taiwan have benefited from a huge boom in artificial intelligence (AI) which has pushed up their profits.

In India, AI, or the new economy broadly, is a major missing piece of its growth story.

"Many of India's large caps [big companies] represent a bygone economic era," Bernstein Research said in a note recently. "Most are not investing in the future, but consolidating their past, often expecting policy to continue shielding them from global competition."

And its smaller companies are yet to reach a scale that will attract foreign institutional funds.

While Indian companies are investing in data centres and chip fabrication, the country has not produced a global giant like OpenAI, Anthropic or even China's DeepSeek - this is where the largest share of the profits in the AI value chain lie.

Foreign investor interest will only return to India meaningfully if it can build globally competitive industries in these emerging areas, according to Bernstein.

"We are seeing early signs of this in areas such as space, defence, semiconductors, and deep-tech innovation, but most remain too small to materially influence capital allocation decisions over much of this decade."

There are many immediate factors that will influence how Indian markets behave going forward.

"Easing geopolitical tensions and relatively attractive valuations could support a revival in FPI [foreign portfolio investor] inflows," according to CareEdge, a brokerage, though trade tensions and higher energy prices remain a “challenge for corporate performance going ahead”.

To what extent corporate margins have been squeezed will become clearer as they start reporting quarterly earnings from this week.

For now, while foreign investors may have given up, Indian savers, even though increasingly more anxious, haven't slowed their monthly investment flows into mutual funds.

The real test will be whether this resilience survives a deeper correction in the future.

articles.title: Dread presenting at work? Read these tips before your next meeting
articles.summary: Dani Payne would have panic attacks at the thought of presenting - now she does it most days.
articles.body:
Dani Payne was so anxious about public speaking, she had a doctor's note to excuse her from presenting at school and university.

Now aged 28 with a job in politics at a cross-party think tank, she's spoken in parliament, sits on discussion panels and presents social media videos.

"Most days I do some form of public speaking," she says. "I wouldn't have believed that at 15."

Want to get better, or simply get started? Here are five ways to help you nail your presentation or speech.

Payne, from Exeter, says she stopped any form of public speaking after developing a severe anxiety disorder and experiencing panic attacks.

But looking back, she says avoiding it didn't help her build "coping skills or resilience you need later in life".

"The more you avoid what you're anxious about, the more you're anxious about it."

In her second year of university she was invited to give a talk on a subject she was passionate about and realised: "I was losing out on opportunities that I felt really strongly about."

She presented research she had carried out for her dissertation on sexual misconduct in academic fieldwork settings and that was the start of her getting over her fear.

"Picking something you genuinely feel passionately about will always make it easier to speak about in front of other people," she says.

Her advice is to pick a topic you feel strongly about and look for or create opportunities to speak about it.

Daisy Schofield, a 32-year-old documentary producer and journalist, had her first panic attack at university during a presentation, she tells Woman's Hour .

She managed to avoid public speaking until she got her first job and had to present company statistics on Teams every Monday.

To build her confidence, Schofield practises by using an app on her phone to create a fake audience in a virtual reality headset she bought online for £10.

"It makes practising feel much more engaging and like the real thing, compared to practising at home on your own, which feels a bit awkward and boring."

Prof Nazanin Derakhshan, a neuroscientist at Birkbeck, University of London, suggests focusing on six breaths per minute before presenting. You can do this by breathing in for five seconds and out for five seconds.

"It can improve the brain-heart communication and the more in harmony they are, the better we feel about ourselves."

Viv Groskop, a stand-up comedian, writer and public speaking coach advises picking a word that encapsulates what you want your speech to convey.

"It could be something like clarity. No one can ever say that you got that wrong if you were clear.

"So choose something that you can think to yourself afterwards, 'did I set out to be clear? Was I clear? Yes. It's a win.' And every time you choose a different word."

Groskop also advises putting a post-it note on your laptop camera and reminding yourself to look there and not at people on the screen.

"You can hide self-view, resist the temptation to look at it, because it will mean you're looking down, not at people."

Groskop does things that relax her ahead of stand up gigs.

This could be getting a good night sleep, staying hydrated or having time off your phone.

"Always wear something that you can forget about. If you love having your hair done, get your hair done.

"Wear makeup or don't wear makeup, whatever makes you feel comfortable so that you won't be thinking about your appearance."

Derakhshan advises not to focus in on people's faces when presenting, as we can misinterpret their reactions.

"Accept that their facial expression may mean anything, and distract yourself internally from interpreting these facial expressions."

Payne says it's important to remember being good at public speaking does not come "naturally to someone".

"You wouldn't pick up a guitar, and be surprised that you couldn't play a song when you've never picked up a guitar before - public speaking is the exact same thing."

She says to become good at public speaking you need to be bad at it first.

"Particularly if you're early in your career, the people around you are not going to expect you to immediately be a master public speaker the first time you do it."

Groksop says people who are good at public speaking have just been doing it more.

"Many people are spending up to eight hours a day on Teams or Zoom, and if you think about a television newsreader, they've been trained for that."

Derakhshan says being vulnerable is a "big asset" when public speaking.

"We all make mistakes, we all forget things. It's not the end of the world. If you can go back and make a humour of it the audience are quite forgiving and accepting."

articles.title: Border czar Tom Homan clashes with CBS interviewer over migrant deaths, asks for Biden-era data
articles.summary: Border Czar Tom Homan challenged CBS over a "loaded question" about ICE detention deaths, arguing the agency has the highest standards in the industry.
articles.body: Border czar Tom Homan accused a CBS journalist of asking a "loaded question" in a Friday interview about how ICE treats detained illegal migrants, asking him whether he gathered statistics about migrant deaths under the Biden administration. CBS News' immigration correspondent Camilo Montoya-Galvez asked Homan about deaths in ICE custody under the Trump administration, noting that this year could set a "new record high." "We looked at official ICE data, sir, and found that 57 people have died in the agency's custody so far under this administration," Montoya-Galvez said. "In fact, somebody was just reported to have died in ICE custody today by the agency. 2026 could set a new record high in the number of detainees dying. What is being done to prevent that? And I know one partial explanation is that more people are being detained and, so tragically, more people are dying. But that can't be the only explanation, can it be?" "How many people died during the Biden administration?" Homan immediately replied, followed by a long pause. "How many people died in custody during the Biden administration? Do you know?" HOMAN VOWS ICE DETENTION FACILITY 'ISN'T GOING ANYWHERE' DESPITE DEMOCRATS' PUSH TO SHUT IT DOWN "A significant number," Montoya-Galvez replied. "Do you know?" Homan pressed further. "But this is going to be the highest year in 2026," Montoya-Galvez continued. "I'm just asking if the pace continues —" "Do you know how many died during the Biden administration?" Homan pressed again. "I don't have the data here," the CBS interviewer admitted. "Of course you don't," Homan said. "Again, it's another loaded question against the Trump administration." BORDER CZAR TOM HOMAN FIRES BACK AT MARGARET BRENNAN OVER ICE PURSUIT Homan said that ICE maintains the highest standards for detention centers. "We have the highest detention standards in industry, higher than any state or federal institution. Our deaths in custody ... are among the lowest of any state prison or Bureau of Prisons. Numbers are up because our population has doubled in custody. We got over 70 — I think the other day we had like 74,000 in custody," he said. Homan went on to argue that the quality of ICE medical care is so high to the point detainees are helped with medical issues they didn’t even know they had. "So we have more people in custody, and we're dealing with people from third-world nations," he said. "Some of the first doctors they see are our doctors. And matter of fact, no one ever talks about how many lives that ICE saves in detention when they found a serious medical issue that the alien didn't even know about and we treat. When I was ICE director, I think we spent almost a billion dollars on medical care." ‘BAKED TO DEATH’: HOMAN RIPS MEDIA WHILE SHARING HORRIFIC SCENES FROM BORDER ENFORCEMENT CAREER He compared ICE detention to federal or state prisons. "Again, it's unfortunate, and it's sad when anybody dies. I don't want to see anybody die, but we do everything we can to give them the best medical care that we can provide. And again, highest detention standards," Homan said. "I think if you look at deaths in custody compared to state prisons or federal penitentiaries, I think we're one of the lowest. At least the last time I looked at the data — it was probably a couple years ago — we're the lowest." Theo Wold, a former acting assistant attorney general and deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy during President Donald Trump's first administration, criticized Montoya-Galvez's questions in comments to Fox News Digital. "This is what passes for journalism in modern America — a reporter comes prepared with gotcha questions but no backup data," he said. "The purpose isn’t to inform the public (which ought to be the goal of journalism), it’s to manufacture ideological sound bites for the nightly news." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "No one wants in-custody deaths, but no administration can avoid them," Wold added. "The Trump Administration has more than doubled Biden-era enforcement, which means more individuals detained and more in-custody deaths, most often through no fault of ICE or its enforcement officers."

articles.title: Luxury fashion designers found shot dead in California as family reportedly reveals troubling lead-up
articles.summary: Fashion designers Bryan Walker and Michelle Min were found shot dead outside their California home as relatives reportedly revealed troubling details about the days before their deaths.
articles.body: The husband and wife behind a California luxury clothing brand were found shot dead outside their hillside home, as relatives reportedly revealed troubling details about the days before their deaths. Oakland police confirmed to Fox News Digital that Bryan Walker and Michelle Min were the two people found dead on Oct. 2 in the 400 block of Panoramic Way. The couple founded women’s luxury apparel company Bryn Walker. Min’s brother, Paul Min, told the Los Angeles Times he believes Walker fatally shot his sister before turning the gun on himself. Police have not confirmed that account. "This remains an active and ongoing investigation. No additional details are being provided at this time," Oakland police told Fox News Digital. KANSAS CONVICTED FELON, SEX OFFENDER ALLEGEDLY KILLS FELLOW FAMILY MEMBERS BEFORE TAKING HIS OWN LIFE: POLICE Paul Min described a troubling decline in his brother-in-law after he allegedly lost millions of dollars in risky financial ventures, according to the outlet. He called Walker the "most honest, responsible, hardworking guy you have ever known" and struggled to reconcile the suspected violence with the man he had known and loved for nearly four decades, the outlet reported. TIKTOK INFLUENCER WHO ACCUSED ESTRANGED HUSBAND OF PEDOPHILIA FOUND DEAD IN POSSIBLE MURDER-SUICIDE Min said he and his sister agreed Walker needed psychiatric help after Walker allegedly suggested that the three of them "end things." Michelle Min was planning to have her husband admitted for psychiatric treatment on the day of the shooting, her brother told the outlet. ‘MARVELOUS MRS. MAISEL’ SET DECORATOR SLAIN, HUSBAND FOUND DEAD IN FAMILY ALREADY SCARRED BY HOME KILLING Police have not confirmed the family’s claims about Walker’s mental health, financial losses or a possible motive. Bryn Walker has been based in Berkeley since 1992 and designs and produces its clothing in the San Francisco Bay Area, according to the company’s website. The brand says it operates six company-owned stores and supplies roughly 1,000 boutiques nationwide. Its store directory lists two Berkeley locations and a shop in Vineyard Haven, Massachusetts, on Martha’s Vineyard. Fox News Digital also reached out to Berkeley police for comment. articles.title: Christa Pike's lawyers push for commuted sentence after botched execution
articles.summary: Attorneys for Christa Pike, who survived a botched execution in Tennessee last week, have renewed their push for the state to commute her death sentence.
articles.body:
Christa Pike , the death row inmate who last week survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her , remained hospitalized on a ventilator Monday, according to her attorney.

He said it was still unclear whether Pike would regain consciousness but urged the state to "take death off the table" by commuting her sentence, renewing an earlier request that the governor denied before her botched lethal injection .

"The least that could happen now is that we at least take death off the table and start looking for what the future could be for her," attorney Steve Ferrell, of the Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, told "CBS Mornings."

Ferrell added that he and the rest of Pike's legal team were "certainly willing to discuss that with the governor, with whoever could make that decision."

He told "CBS Mornings" that, although Pike was alive, her condition was considered critical and hospital staff continued to work to clear her body of the lethal drug pentobarbital. Even if she were to wake up, her future would be uncertain, he added.

"It may still be a long time before she's able to participate in the legal process," said Ferrell.

However, in hopes of preventing the possibility of Tennessee trying to execute Pike a second time, which is historically what has happened to inmates who've survived botched execution attempts, he said Pike's legal team would push for the state to commute her death sentence to life in prison.

Pike has been incarcerated, largely in isolation, for three decades. She was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of her former classmate, Colleen Slemmer, who was 19 when she was killed. Pike was 18, which made her the youngest person in the country's modern death penalty era to be executed for a crime committed at 18, 19 or 20.

In the aftermath of Pike's botched execution, Tennessee's Department of Correction commissioner stepped down . Meanwhile, Gov. Bill Lee canceled the state's next and last execution scheduled for this year and said he'd ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review" to determine what went wrong; Lee also went on to tell reporters at a briefing that "so far as we know, the Department of Correction followed exactly the protocol as outlined."

Tennessee's execution protocol has come under scrutiny before, and, in 2022, prompted the state to pause executions and investigate its lethal injection procedure. It resumed executions in 2025, carrying out three of them with a new lethal cocktail that consisted of a single drug, pentobarbital, rather than the combination of three it used formerly. But issues returned to Tennessee's death chamber earlier this year, when correctional staff botched the planned execution of Tony Carruthers , also by lethal injection, after failing to establish an IV line.

At least seven U.S. inmates, including Carruthers, have survived failed lethal injections due to issues with their IV. But Pike's survival was unprecedented, an expert told CBS News on Friday, because she had lived after actually receiving lethal drugs. Pike received two doses.

"That fact alone tells us that something went seriously wrong in the execution chamber," said Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. "It is an unprecedented event in the modern death penalty era."

Because of Tennessee's past mistakes while trying to put inmates to death, and because botched executions have happened increasingly often in other states, too, in recent years, leading to numerous accusations of torture against corrections officials, Pike had said she was "nervous about the process" in the days leading up to her execution date. Her attorneys had shared those concerns as well in their appeals filings, but, as Ferrell said in a statement after Pike's injection failed: "All of this was predicted, and the court did nothing."

articles.standfirst: Apostas podem ser feitas até as 20h em lotéricas ou pela internet.
articles.summary: Apostas podem ser feitas até as 20h em lotéricas ou pela internet.
articles.body:
O concurso 3.067 da Mega-Sena pode pagar um prêmio de R$ 92 milhões para os apostadores que acertarem as seis dezenas. O sorteio ocorre às 21h desta terça-feira (6), em São Paulo.

No concurso do último sábado (3), nenhuma aposta acertou a faixa principal e o valor acumulou.

O g1 transmite todos os sorteios das Loterias Caixa, ao vivo . A transmissão começa momentos antes de cada dia de concursos, no site e no canal do g1 no YouTube .

A aposta mínima para a Mega-Sena custa R$ 6 e pode ser realizada também pela internet – saiba como fazer a sua aposta online .

Volante da Mega-Sena — Foto: Ana Marin/g1

As apostas podem ser realizadas até as 20h (horário de Brasília) em qualquer lotérica do país ou por meio do site e aplicativo Loterias Caixa, disponíveis em smartphones, computadores e outros dispositivos.

Já os bolões digitais poderão ser comprados até as 20h30, exclusivamente pelo portal Loterias Online e pelo aplicativo.

Ainda segundo a Caixa, para os sorteios realizados aos domingos as apostas simples podem ser efetuadas até as 22h de sábado por meio das unidades lotéricas, pelo Portal Loterias Caixa e do aplicativo Loterias Caixa.

A comercialização dos Bolões Caixa nos canais eletrônicos, nesse caso, acontece até às 10h45 do domingo, quinze minutos antes da realização dos sorteios.

O pagamento da aposta online pode ser realizado via PIX, cartão de crédito ou pelo internet banking, para correntistas da Caixa. É preciso ter 18 anos ou mais para participar.

A probabilidade de vencer em cada concurso varia de acordo com o número de dezenas jogadas e do tipo de aposta realizada. Para um jogo simples, com apenas seis dezenas, que custa R$ 6, a probabilidade de ganhar o prêmio milionário é de 1 em 50.063.860, segundo a Caixa.

Já para uma aposta com 20 dezenas (limite máximo), com o preço de R$ 232.560,00, a probabilidade de acertar o prêmio é de 1 em 1.292, ainda de acordo com a instituição.

articles.title: Cidades paraguaias estão entre as que mais votaram em Flávio Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Em algumas localidades paraguaias, candidato do PL superou 90% dos votos válidos, enquanto Lula ficou abaixo de 10%.
articles.summary: Em algumas localidades paraguaias, candidato do PL superou 90% dos votos válidos, enquanto Lula ficou abaixo de 10%.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula — Foto: Evaristo Sá/AFP e Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

A corrida eleitoral foi marcada pela polarização entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro na disputa pela Presidência. No entanto, apesar da disputa acirrada que levou a eleição para o segundo turno, o Paraguai desponta como um dos países com mais cidades onde um dos dois candidatos abriu larga vantagem sobre o adversário.

Na cidade de Salto del Guairá , a menos de 20 minutos da fronteira com Mato Grosso do Sul, Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu 496 votos, o equivalente a 94,48% dos votos válidos . Lula, por sua vez, teve apenas 19 votos (3,62%).

Em Concepción , no centro do país, Flávio também concentrou a maior parte dos votos: foram 32, ou 91,43% do total. Lula recebeu apenas dois votos, correspondentes a 5,71%.

Já em Ciudad del Este , na fronteira com Foz do Iguaçu, Flávio teve 89,45% dos votos, contra 8,07% de Lula.

O resultado se repete em outras cidades paraguaias, com Flávio aparecendo à frente de Lula em diferentes pontos do país. A votação no exterior é contabilizada pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), que disponibiliza os resultados por localidade e seção eleitoral.

Apesar das diferenças expressivas em algumas cidades, o resultado no Paraguai faz parte de um cenário mais muito amplo da eleição presidencial de 2026, que terminou o primeiro turno com Flávio Bolsonaro com 47,03% dos votos e Lula com 45,16%, ambos classificados para a segunda etapa da disputa.

Os votos deste primeiro turno mostram um resultado diferente em alguns países quando comparado às eleições de 2022, quando Lula enfrentou o pai de Flávio, Jair Bolsonaro.

No Kuwait, por exemplo, onde Bolsonaro foi o mais votado há quatro anos, o petista venceu desta vez. Na Tailândia, o movimento foi inverso: o país que deu a maior votação ao atual presidente em 2022 teve Flávio como o mais votado em 2026.

Lula também voltou a vencer em países como Portugal, França, Alemanha e Reino Unido. Flávio, por sua vez, foi o mais votado no Japão e em Israel, onde seu pai havia vencido na eleição anterior.

Portugal : Lula voltou a vencer, com 52,45%. No primeiro turno de 2022, o petista recebeu 60,4%.

Israel : Flávio foi o mais votado, com 74,40%. Jair Bolsonaro venceu no país em 2022, com 46%.

Estados Unidos : Flávio foi o mais votado com 61,1% dos votos. Em 2022, Jair Bolsonaro venceu por 57,9%.

Alemanha : Lula venceu com 74,58%. Em 2022 o petista também saiu vitorioso, com 69,4%.

França : Lula venceu por 78,39%. Em 2022, o atual preseidente também venceu por 77,6%.

articles.title: Dá para emendar o feriado de 12 de outubro? Entenda as regras | G1
articles.standfirst: Data cai em uma segunda-feira e garante três dias seguidos de descanso para quem folga aos fins de semana; veja quando é possível emendar e quais são os direitos de quem for escalado.
articles.summary: Data cai em uma segunda-feira e garante três dias seguidos de descanso para quem folga aos fins de semana; veja quando é possível emendar e quais são os direitos de quem trabalha.
articles.body:
Nossa Senhora Aparecida — Foto: Divulgação/Santuário Nacional

Muitos trabalhadores já estão de olho no tão esperado “feriadão”, que chega na próxima segunda-feira (12), Dia de Nossa Senhora Aparecida, padroeira do Brasil , e também Dia das Crianças. A data é um feriado nacional e garante, em regra, um dia de descanso aos trabalhadores.

O fato de as duas celebrações ocorrerem no mesmo dia é apenas uma coincidência: o feriado é referente somente a Nossa Senhora Aparecida, padroeira do Brasil. O Dia das Crianças, apesar de ser uma data comemorativa mais antiga, não é feriado. ( veja como surgiu a data )

Como cai no início da semana, a data garante três dias consecutivos de descanso para quem não trabalha aos sábados e domingos. Veja como fica o calendário:

10 de outubro (sábado): folga para quem não trabalha aos fins de semana;

11 de outubro (domingo): folga para quem não trabalha aos fins de semana;

12 de outubro (segunda-feira): feriado nacional de Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

Ao todo, ainda restam quatro feriados nacionais em 2026 — e três deles podem render um fim de semana prolongado, aumentando os dias de descanso. ( veja calendário abaixo )

Vale lembrar que, mesmo nos feriados nacionais, nem todos os trabalhadores são dispensados. A legislação permite o funcionamento de atividades consideradas essenciais e de outras categorias autorizadas a trabalhar nesses dias.

⚠️ Nesses casos, quem trabalhar no feriado pode ter direito a remuneração em dobro ou a uma folga compensatória , conforme as regras aplicáveis à categoria.

O g1 conversou com advogados especialistas em direito trabalhista para ajudar a entender as regras.

🤔 Meu chefe pode me obrigar a trabalhar durante o feriado?

💰 Remuneração em dobro ou folga? Quem define?

❌ Faltei ao trabalho, apesar de ter sido escalado. Posso ser demitido por justa causa?

⚠️ As regras são diferentes para empregado fixo e temporário?

✍🏼 Como funciona no caso do trabalhador intermitente?

📆 Quais são os próximos feriados de 2026?

1. Meu chefe pode me obrigar a trabalhar durante o feriado?

Sim. Apesar de o artigo 70 da CLT proibir atividades profissionais durante feriados nacionais, a legislação abre exceções para serviços considerados essenciais , como setores da indústria, comércio, transportes, comunicações, serviços funerários e atividades ligadas à segurança, entre outros.

Além disso, o empregador pode solicitar que o funcionário trabalhe durante o feriado quando houver uma Convenção Coletiva de Trabalho — acordo previamente firmado entre empregadores e sindicatos.

Para quem trabalha no feriado, a legislação garante o pagamento em dobro ou a compensação com folga em outro dia.

"Se houver banco de horas, também é possível lançar essas horas trabalhadas, nos termos do acordo individual ou coletivo", explica Ana Gabriela Burlamaqui, advogada trabalhista e sócia do AC Burlamaqui Consultores.

3. Remuneração em dobro ou folga? Quem define?

A definição do tipo de compensação — pagamento em dobro ou concessão de folga compensatória — geralmente é determinada em acordo firmado entre empregador e sindicato.

Na ausência da Convenção Coletiva de Trabalho, a decisão pode ser negociada entre empregador e funcionário. No entanto, é importante que as duas partes estejam de acordo e que a compensação escolhida esteja em conformidade com a legislação.

"O empregador não pode decidir de forma unilateral. Se houver um acordo ou convenção coletiva prevendo a compensação por folga, essa regra prevalece; caso não exista, o pagamento em dobro pelo trabalho no feriado é obrigatório", afirma Elisa Alonso, advogada trabalhista e sócia do RCA Advogados.

4. Faltei ao trabalho, apesar de ter sido escalado. Posso ser demitido por justa causa?

Depende. A ausência pode ser caracterizada como insubordinação — ou seja, desobediência a um superior hierárquico.

"Mas a dispensa por justa causa, em geral, não decorre de um fato isolado, mas de um comportamento faltoso de forma reiterada", afirma Ana Gabriela Burlamaqui, advogada trabalhista.

Assim, a demissão por justa causa geralmente resulta de um processo que inclui advertências formais e tentativas de correção de comportamento.

Em caso de expediente normal, o empregado poderá sofrer outras penalidades administrativas como o desconto do dia não trabalhado, que será considerado falta injustificada.

"A falta injustificada deve ser repreendida. No entanto, para a caracterização de justa causa, outros fatores precisam ser analisados, como a recorrência da conduta, o impacto causado à empresa e a função exercida pelo empregado", completa a advogada trabalhista Elisa Alonso.

5. As regras são diferentes para empregado fixo e temporário?

As regras básicas sobre trabalho em feriados aplicam-se tanto a empregados fixos quanto temporários, incluindo o direito ao pagamento em dobro ou folga compensatória .

No entanto, trabalhadores contratados em regime temporário podem ter condições específicas previstas em contrato.

6. Como funciona no caso do trabalhador intermitente?

Para o trabalhador contratado em regime de trabalho intermitente — previsão legal incluída na CLT pela Reforma Trabalhista de 2017 —, o pagamento pelos dias trabalhados em feriados deve ser acordado no momento da contratação.

O contrato deve especificar o valor da hora trabalhada, que já precisa considerar os adicionais devidos por trabalho em feriados ou por horas extras.

Dessa forma, o trabalhador intermitente recebe exatamente o valor previamente combinado para os dias efetivamente trabalhados, incluindo feriados, explica o advogado Luís Nicoli.

7. Quais são os próximos feriados de 2026?

Depois de outubro, a próxima oportunidade de folga será em 28 de outubro, Dia do Servidor Público. A data é considerada ponto facultativo no âmbito federal.

➡️ Na prática, estados e municípios podem adotar a data em seus próprios calendários como feriado, conforme regulamentação local, o que pode abrir espaço para uma emenda e prolongar o descanso.

Depois disso, novembro chega com três feriados nacionais. O primeiro deles será em 2 de novembro, Dia de Finados.

O feriado cairá novamente em uma segunda-feira , o que permitirá três dias seguidos de descanso para os trabalhadores que folgam aos fins de semana.

Quem for escalado para trabalhar no feriado terá direito, em regra, ao pagamento em dobro ou a uma folga compensatória.

Veja abaixo os próximos feriados nacionais e os dias da semana em que caem:

15 de novembro — Proclamação da República (domingo)

20 de novembro — Dia da Consciência Negra (sexta-feira)

Confira também os próximos pontos facultativos, que podem resultar em folga em alguns casos:

28 de outubro — Dia do Servidor Público (quarta-feira)

24 de dezembro — véspera de Natal, após as 13h (quinta-feira)

31 de dezembro — véspera de Ano Novo, após as 13h (quinta-feira)

articles.title: Privacy fears push vacation spot to consider ban on favorite accessory for travelers
articles.summary: AI smart glasses at beaches, parks, museums and shopping centers could be banned in Norway over growing concerns about the hidden recording of citizens.
articles.body: Travelers could face new restrictions on smart glasses in one popular European destination. The government of Norway plans to propose a temporary ban on AI-enabled glasses in certain public places, according to a press release from the Norwegian Ministry of Digitalization and Public Governance. The restrictions could apply to places that travelers regularly visit — including beaches, parks, museums, shopping centers and public events, the press release said. CRIME, KIDNAPPINGS AND DRONE ATTACKS FLAGGED IN US WARNING FOR BORDER REGION Smart glasses can be equipped with cameras and microphones capable of taking photos and recording video or audio. Norwegian officials said they are concerned the technology could allow people to be recorded without realizing it. "We do not want a society where people are concerned about hidden sound recordings, photography and filming in places and in situations where they are used to being without being monitored," said Torgeir Micaelssen, minister of Digitalization and Public Administration. The proposed restrictions are not yet in effect. The government plans to bring legislation before Norway's parliament, known as the Storting, as soon as possible. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Officials are still determining exactly which devices and locations would be covered, including whether the rules would apply only to AI-enabled glasses or to other wearable technology capable of recording, the press release noted. There are concerns that the technology could allow people to be recorded without realizing it. The government said it is not seeking a complete ban on smart glasses. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES The devices could still be used privately and in certain settings where other people are not at risk of being recorded without their consent. The proposal comes as privacy concerns surrounding smart glasses are also being debated in the United States. California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently vetoed legislation that would have penalized people for using smart glasses to record others without permission in places such as changing rooms and doctors' offices, according to The Associated Press (AP). The measure also would have required smart glasses and other wearable recording devices beginning in 2028 to include a light or another feature signaling when audio or video was being captured, the AP reported. Newsom said the bill's definition of a wearable recording device was too general. He also noted that California already has laws prohibiting people from recording others without permission in places where privacy is generally expected, according to the AP. Under the proposed legislation, people who secretly recorded someone in covered circumstances could have faced fines of up to $1,500 or possible prison time. The Associated Press contributed reporting.

articles.title: Police clash with Kosovo protesters over bid to curb Hague war crimes court
articles.summary: The political dispute over the court has become a factor in negotiations to hold a new presidential election.
articles.body:
Police have clashed with protesters outside Kosovo’s Parliament over plans to limit the powers of a Hague-based war crimes court.

The violence broke out on Monday evening after Parliament ended its session without passing the proposed changes, which concerned the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a court dedicated to crimes committed during the Kosovo War from 1998 to 2000.

Founded in 2015, the court is an independent part of Kosovo’s judicial system, based in The Hague and staffed internationally.

Critics, however, have accused the court’s verdicts of being overly punitive. The amendments before Parliament would limit sentences to 15 years, allow sentences to be served in Kosovo and permit appeals to the self-declared republic’s Supreme Court.

The changes passed a first reading earlier on Monday, but Parliament adjourned before a second vote could be held.

Several hundred protesters had gathered outside the Parliament building in Pristina, including supporters and veterans of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), the ethnic Albanian rebel force that fought Serbian troops in the war.

Some tried to block lawmakers from leaving after the session ended. Police used tear gas and water cannons in an attempt to disperse the protesters, some of whom threw flares and firecrackers.

Naser Syla, the emergency director at a hospital in Pristina, told The Associated Press news agency that 12 people were injured, including 11 civilians.

The legislation follows the September 16 convictions of former President Hashim Thaci and three other former KLA commanders for war crimes.

Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison. His co-defendants received prison terms ranging from 13 to 25 years. They have all denied the charges.

The rulings prompted weeks of protests and were unanimously condemned by Kosovo’s Parliament in late September.

The question of reforming the court has also become tied to the political battle over Kosovo’s presidency.

Kosovo’s Constitutional Court has ruled that the self-declared republic has until October 6 to elect a president. If lawmakers fail to do so, Parliament will be dissolved, and Kosovo will face another early election.

The Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), the largest opposition party and sponsor of the bill, has hinged its support for electing a president to the successful passage of the changes.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti’s governing Vetevendosje party, or the Self-Determination Movement, wants the presidential vote to take place first.

Kurti backed allowing the bill to proceed but told Parliament on Monday that the changes had been rushed.

He has also said the appeals process should be used to challenge the controversial September convictions.

Kosovo created the Specialist Chambers under pressure from Western allies to prosecute alleged crimes by KLA members.

It was based outside Kosovo partly due to concerns about political pressure and threats to witnesses.

The court remains deeply contentious in Kosovo, where many people regard the KLA as the force that fought Serbian repression and led the self-declared republic towards declaring independence.

The 1998-99 war killed about 13,000 people, most of them ethnic Albanians, and forced about one million Kosovo Albanians from their homes.

The conflict ended after a 78-day NATO bombing campaign against Serbian forces. Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008, but Belgrade does not recognise its sovereignty.

articles.title: Jeffrey Archer, bestselling UK novelist and scandal-plagued politician, dies aged 86
articles.summary: Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, has died aged 86, his publisher HarperCollins said on Monday.
articles.body: Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, has died aged 86, his publisher HarperCollins said on Monday. Archer sold over 300 million copies worldwide and was known for pacy thrillers like his 1976 debut “Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less” and 1979’s “Kane & Abel.” His final novel, “Adam and Eve,” is due to be published on Tuesday. Kate Elton, HarperCollins’ UK CEO and Archer’s editor, said in a statement: “We’re all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers — and a true friend.” Archer was also a prominent Conservative politician, who briefly served as a lawmaker before becoming a senior party official under then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s. But he was as well-known for his very public downfall. In 1987, Archer sued the Daily Star tabloid for saying he had paid a woman for sex, winning a then-record £500,000 ($660,450) in damages. The case returned to the public eye when he was selected as the Conservative candidate to become London’s first elected mayor in 1999. A former friend accused him of lying and Archer was eventually charged with perjury and perverting the course of justice, convicted and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. He served two years, during which time he wrote “A Prison Diary.” Archer trial notorious for judge’s summing up The trial of Archer’s libel case, which was heard in front of a jury, became notorious for the judge’s summing up of evidence given by Archer’s wife Mary. “Remember Mary Archer in the witness box,” the judge, Bernard Caulfield, told the jury. “Your vision of her will probably never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance?” And, of Archer, he added: “Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel?” Archer’s reputation as one of the most colourful figures in British public life did no harm to his literary career. His books were sold in 119 countries, HarperCollins said. He spent a total of five-and-a-half years on the New York Times bestseller lists. He was due to speak about his final novel this weekend at the Cheltenham Literature Festival and had recently appeared on radio shows to promote the book. HarperCollins said he had died suddenly and peacefully, “between writing sessions.”
