articles.title: Moroccan journalists recount years of surveillance amid new Amnesty claim
articles.summary: Amnesty cites a whistleblower’s account of how Morocco allegedly uses surveillance to silence journalists.
articles.body:
Rabat, Morocco – “I was surveilled not because of a specific article. I was investigating land dispossession in Morocco. I then learned I was a Pegasus target,” Omar Radi, a journalist and human rights defender, told Al Jazeera, referring to the mobile surveillance tool developed by Israeli company NSO Group.

The findings emerged in June 2020, when Amnesty International Security Lab examined his phone. Radi, now based in Germany, said he had spent two years, from 2018 to 2020, noticing signs including his phone’s battery draining quickly, its temperature rising and the network slowing down.

The physical surveillance, he said, was barely discreet.

“They came every day to get a daily report from the parking attendants in my street, the shops I used to go to, and my friends,” he said. “I would sometimes turn around and walk towards the people following me to take photographs, but they ran quickly and hid their faces.”

His case is among four detailed in a new Amnesty International report, We Start With the Verdict: Inside Morocco’s Surveillance Machine, produced with 14 media organisations and coordinated by the international network of journalists Forbidden Stories.

The other three are Fouad Abdelmoumni, a veteran activist; Abdessadak El Bouchattaoui, a human rights lawyer; and Hicham Mansouri, a journalist in exile who had been imprisoned in 2015 on charges of adultery and sexual exploitation, which Amnesty describes as trumped-up.

The report draws on interviews with a whistleblower using the pseudonym Safir, a former employee of Morocco’s General Directorate for Territorial Surveillance (DGST). Amnesty said it corroborated key parts of Safir’s testimony with independent sources, technical evidence and interviews with 10 people identified as surveillance targets, including Radi.

“The Amnesty report connected many dots as to what I was living and feeling while I was under tight surveillance,” Radi said.

“It explains the extraordinary aspect of my police interrogations and my trial, where many of my rights weren’t respected, because even the judicial police and the judges were under monitoring,” he added.

Amnesty identifies the DGST as the agency behind the deployment of Pegasus spyware in Morocco and documents what it describes as abuses of the spyware against activists and journalists between 2017 and 2021.

Morocco has previously rejected Amnesty’s allegations that its authorities used Pegasus to target journalists, activists and other critics.

In statements issued in 2020 and 2022, Moroccan authorities challenged Amnesty to provide material evidence supporting its claims.

Amnesty said it wrote to Moroccan authorities four weeks before publishing its latest report and invited them to respond, but received no response.

Al Jazeera also sought comment from Moroccan officials but had not received a response at the time of publication.

Moroccan media have also challenged the latest report. Le360 cited arguments that the presence of a phone number in Pegasus targeting records does not, by itself, prove that a device was infected or establish who ordered an alleged attack.

The outlet also argued that Amnesty had not provided the conclusive technical and material evidence Moroccan authorities had demanded.

The report says Morocco’s Pegasus operations were fully active by October 2017, pointing to the case of human rights lawyer El Bouchattaoui, whose number was entered into the system in September 2017 and selected for targeting weeks before he received an infection link by text message.

Amnesty said its analysis of Pegasus records matched 103 Moroccan phone numbers to individuals identified as potential targets between September and December 2017. Of those, 65 were identifiable as civil society members, including 34 human rights defenders, 22 journalists and media workers, five lawyers and four academics.

According to Amnesty, Safir described a surveillance apparatus that combined digital and physical methods. Targeted individuals were secretly filmed and recorded in detention, offices, cars, cafes and even bedrooms, he said.

Phone shops, he added, were coopted to sell targets devices infected with spyware. Neighbours of human rights defenders, he said, were recruited as informants to file daily reports on their movements.

Safir also described the use of remote control systems (RCS) at internet cafes. Field agents would identify which cafe a target was visiting, he said, giving the DGST access to activity on machines it had already infected and allowing an operator to track calls, read messages, access photographs and record audio.

The report says similar tactics were used against activist Abdelmoumni, who was secretly filmed at home with his fiancee in 2021. Abdelmoumni said he believed the footage was captured through a hidden camera in an air-conditioning unit, based on the recording’s angle.

Safir described the episode as a “textbook case” of a DGST surveillance and cleanup operation designed to leave no trace.

Journalists describe pressure and intimidation

Taoufik Bouachrine, one of Morocco’s best-known journalists and host of the Talk on Politics podcast, was not named in Amnesty’s report but described a similar pattern.

“In Morocco, as in all Arab countries, inventive methods are used to silence journalists and deter them from investigative journalism, particularly when it concerns the unlawful exercise of power, financial corruption, and the intertwining of political authority and money,” he told Al Jazeera.

The first method, he said, is fabricating criminal cases against journalists, “often involving allegations of sexual misconduct in a conservative society that amount to a journalist’s moral execution”.

The second, he said, is a smear campaign run through armies of online trolls and operatives who target journalists and their families.

Bouachrine, 57, was arrested in 2018 on charges of rape and human trafficking and sentenced to 15 years in prison. He has denied the charges, saying his prosecution was tied to his journalism.

The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found Bouachrine’s detention arbitrary and said he had been subjected to judicial harassment. The European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for his release, along with other journalists tried on similar charges.

He served more than six years before being released under a royal pardon. By then, Akhbar Al-Youm, the newspaper he founded, had already closed. Bouachrine said authorities had cut off its advertising revenue.

“This is another method of destroying investigative journalism,” he added, “turning off the advertising tap and leaving a newspaper to die slowly.”

images.caption: Moroccan journalist Omar Radi has spoken about being targeted with Pegasus spyware, amid allegations of surveillance against journalists, activists and other critics that authorities have denied [File: Abdeljalil Bounhar/AP Photo]

articles.title: UK weather: Temperatures drop as rain and cloud sweep in
articles.summary: Tuesday will see cool air spread across the UK ahead of a noticeable drop in temperatures for all by Wednesday.
articles.body:
After weeks of unusually warm weather, autumn is finally set to make its presence felt on Tuesday as cooler air sweeps across the UK from the north-west.

Temperatures will plunge from the low 20s to the mid-teens. Wednesday could be the first day since June when temperatures stay below 20C across the whole of the country.

A spell of rain and stronger winds will accompany the colder air, adding to the autumnal feel.

But the cooler spell is not expected to last, with temperatures set to rise towards average over the weekend.

Noticeable change to October's warm start

Cloud, rain and strong winds affecting parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland will spread further south on Tuesday.

This band of rain and cloud will usher in much cooler air, setting the scene for a distinctly autumnal Wednesday.

Temperatures on Tuesday could still reach 19-21C in the south-east, but northern and western areas will be much cooler, with highs mainly in the low to mid-teens.

The change will be particularly noticeable after such a warm start to October with Monday offering a final taste of summer-like conditions for southern and central parts of England and Wales

Temperatures fall further into Wednesday and Thursday

By Wednesday, the autumn chill will be firmly established and it is expected to be the first day since 11 June when temperatures fail to reach 20C anywhere in the UK.

Cooler north-westerly winds will bring sunshine and scattered showers to many areas, while rain could be heavy and persistent for a time across south-eastern England and East Anglia.

Temperatures will fall into the mid-teens across much of England and Wales. Scotland could see highs of just 10-13C.

The wind will also make it feel colder than the thermometer suggests, particularly around eastern coastal areas.

While mid-teen temperatures are perfectly normal for early October, the sharp contrast with the warmth of recent weeks is likely to make the change feel much more dramatic.

Thursday will start off chilly with mist and fog patches along with frost in places.

However, the day will bring some welcome sunshine as a temporary area of high pressure moves across the UK.

Temperatures are expected to reach around 14-16C in southern areas, with Scotland struggling to get much above 10-12C.

By Friday, Atlantic weather systems will bring further rain and stronger winds, although temperatures will recover slightly, reaching 16-18C across much of the south.

The cooler spell is not expected to last and temperatures should return towards average over the weekend and even slightly above average again next week.

But after such an extended period of warmth, this week's change may be the moment autumn finally feels as though it has arrived.

You can check your local weather forecast, including the expected feels-like temperatures, on the BBC Weather website and app .

articles.title: Student protests erupt at Cornell over mishandling of gang-rape allegations
articles.summary: Hall housing Michael Kotlikoff’s office spray painted as demonstrators demand resignation of college president
articles.body:
Mass protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday, with students criticizing officials' handling of gang-rape allegations , demanding the president's resignation and painting "SMASH THE PATRIARCHY" on an administration building.

Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration, sparked by the high-profile case of a former student known as Jane Doe, who said in a recent lawsuit that she was plied with drugs and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The case has prompted international outrage and intense scrutiny of college fraternities and sexual violence on US campuses.

Protesters shouted , "Ban the frats" and held signs saying, "At Cornell, rapists are safer than women" and "Stop rape culture." Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell's president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe and chanting , "Kotlikoff, resign!"

The demonstration took place after some students had smashed a glass door at the entrance of Day Hall, a building that houses the president's office, and painted messages on the facade at approximately 3am on Monday, the Cornell Daily Sun reported .

The messages in red paint read "SMASH THE PATRIARCHY" and "AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED". The security camera above one of the messages was also painted over.

The students who graffitied the building said in a statement to the student newspaper that they were protesting "the global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place".

"We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the center of Cornell's administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual," the statement added. The students' painted message was a reference to arguments that campus officials had treated pro-Palestine protesters more harshly than students accused of sexual misconduct, with four student demonstrators suspended in 2024, according to the Cornell Daily Sun.

Kyle Kimball, a Cornell spokesperson, condemned vandalism in a statement on Monday.

"We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer," Kimball said. "We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law."

The student activists defended their actions in a manifesto obtained by the student publication. "We reject the dogma that would condemn our actions this morning as violent while excusing rape," they wrote. "Property damage is not violent; condoning rape is."

The demonstrations escalated as Cornell faces widespread backlash for its handling of Jane Doe's case, with critics saying the university had been too lenient with the accused men and had failed the victim.

According to lawyers for Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. Jane Doe dropped out of Cornell after the incident.

A third fraternity member, who had already graduated, was barred from the Cornell campus, the New York Times reported on Saturday. Two more were reportedly given suspensions and disciplinary probation.

Two other men, the outlet said, were ordered not to contact the sophomore and required to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write "reflection papers".

The lawsuit claimed that the seven fraternity members allegedly involved in the incident were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell".

The university has said that claim does not accurately reflect what occurred. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing.

One student protester who addressed the crowd on Monday said : "Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support. How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?"

And a professor, according to the AP, said to applause: "Rape should not be inevitable."

Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, who is also under fire for his office's handling of the original allegations, announced last week he was reopening the case. Van Houten said Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were "dramatically different" from the statement she gave to police two years ago. Jane Doe's attorney has pushed back on those claims and accused the DA of failing to do a thorough investigation after the incident.

Kathy Hochul , the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James , the state's attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape at Cornell University.

Kotlikoff, the university president under fire, addressed the case in a video message on Saturday, saying the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included "a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life", Kotlikoff said.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Trump says he will stop using US taxpayer funds for ads
articles.summary: The ads, which tout Trump and his policies, could have violated US laws barring public government funds being spent on political advertising.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has said he will stop using US taxpayer funds to pay for television ads he has fronted, following bipartisan pushback.

"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," he said Monday on social media.

Trump said it is "a rather standard thing to do" but that he has decided to pay for the "Patriotic Ads" himself and with money he raised through his MAGA Inc super political action committee.

The ads, which praise the president and his policies, drew criticism and questions over their legality due to laws against using government money for political ads.

Are Trump's US government funded ads illegal?

There have been more than a dozen ads over recent weeks, with some mentioning Trump's tax cuts, US manufacturing and law and order. In them, Trump also vows to take action against the "deep state" and others he perceives as enemies.

In one ad, Trump says, "We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all".

The ads come just ahead of the pivotal November midterm elections , when Democrats hope to take control of one or both chambers of the US Congress as polls continue to show Trump's approval rating falling. Midterm elections often serve as a verdict on how a president is doing - and typically the party of a sitting president tends to lose seats in Congress.

The White House has pushed back against criticism, calling the ads "educational" and saying they are not propaganda, but rather public service announcements.

They've pointed to previous administrations ads, like those under former Presidents Barack Obama on his healthcare plan and one under former President Joe Biden urging people to get Covid-19 vaccines.

But legal experts say past US government adverts have typically been about public health or national emergencies.

"It's difficult to see what legitimate government purpose is served by spending taxpayer dollars on ads whose only apparent purpose is to promote the president," legal ethics expert Margaret Dylus-Yukins has told the BBC.

Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire introduced a measure, which was blocked by a Republican, denouncing the administration for using government funds for for the ads.

"It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language 'paid for by the U.S. Government,' should not be paid for by the United States government," the measure reads.

The ads have received criticism on both sides of the aisle.

Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday that while "I like the message ... it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars".

Senator John Kennedy, a Republican, said on CBS News on Sunday that politicians should not spend taxpayer funds on promotional ads.

"I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," the Louisiana lawmaker said.

articles.title: MAGA activists protest AI data centers at Big Tech headquarters in San Francisco
articles.summary: The group, called Humans First, advocates for better guardrails on data center construction and AI in general.
articles.body: SAN FRANCISCO — As food delivery workers on e-scooters whizzed past a hulking tour bus parked next to Anthropic’s headquarters in downtown San Francisco on Monday afternoon, software engineers returning from their lunch breaks snapped pictures of a brash slogan bursting out of the bus’ idyllic Americana artwork of farmhouses and fields of grain. “AI Data Center Revolt,” the bus’ detailed wrapping declared, proclaiming its mission to rally communities against wanton data center construction efforts across the country. The bus and its small crew of conservative activists from a group called Humans First had just completed an over 8,000-mile whistle-stop marathon of a road trip on perhaps the most uniting theme today: anti-data-center sentiment. “This technology is being shoved down people’s throats,” said Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, admiring the bus’ artwork from a nearby sidewalk. She said the group aimed to push back against AI giants and their assumption that they can build billions of dollars of AI infrastructure without residents’ input. “That’s not the American way,” she said. Founded this year as a coalition of left- and right-wing activists who worry that the rush to embrace AI is being spearheaded by tech oligarchs steamrolling Americans’ ability to steer the technology, Humans First has since morphed into a conservative-only effort led by Kremer to advocate for better guardrails on data center construction and AI in general. Kremer, a veteran conservative organizer who played noted roles in the tea party and the organization that helped create the rally preceding the Jan. 6, 2021 Capitol attack, has spearheaded cross-country bus trips to extol MAGA talking points and deny the outcome of the 2020 election. Composed of Kremer, her husband, her daughter and her dog, Lovie — “He’s been with me the entire trip,” Kremer said — along with staffers and security guards, the Humans First squad has made more than 35 stops in communities across the country over the past five weeks. The trip culminated in Monday’s visits to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta and Nvidia — widely regarded as the world’s largest and most influential AI companies. Kremer and her daughter, Kylie Jane Kremer, fielded questions from reporters about the tour’s goals and its accomplishments. “I want Big Tech to actually include the American people and allow them to have a seat at the table,” said Kylie Jane, a senior adviser at Humans First. She highlighted the organization’s Data Center Policy, a 13-point charter that emphasizes community control over data center planning, rejects data centers’ role in increasing electricity prices and decries any use of American data centers for unconstitutional surveillance, among other issues. “We’re not anti-AI, we’re not anti-tech, we’re not even anti-data center,” Kylie Jane said. Instead, the team touts a proud populist message: AI development must prioritize Americans, and the historic infrastructure buildout must benefit the communities hosting data centers humming with billions of dollars of business. Yet, during the monthlong tour, much of the nation’s AI discourse shifted dramatically from worries about data centers’ guzzling water to fears that the technology might wipe out billions of people — or the entire species — in the next decade. Recent worries about such risks were catalyzed by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s warning on X that leading AI companies are recklessly speeding toward technological disaster. Amy Kremer said AI’s potential existential threats had clearly struck a nerve with Middle America, with growing numbers of people at Humans First rallies bringing up AI’s risks to society beyond immediate data center impacts. “People across the country are definitely paying attention to the existential risk and what is coming out about that,” Kremer said. On Sunday, Kremer participated in a panel at a gathering of AI luminaries in nearby Berkeley, where she laid out the future of conservative AI approaches to mitigate such potential outcomes. Kremer said she vehemently disagreed with some of the conference’s participants about the idea that AI systems could ever be conscious or have a soul — a belief some Anthropic employees acknowledge as possible. “Personally, I think it’s demonic,” she said, looking toward the Anthropic headquarters. “We are human beings, and we all have souls. And you cannot put a soul in a machine. Part of me feels sad for them that that’s how empty and soulless their lives are.” Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Kremer and her cadre have found thousands of Americans fed up with large AI companies’ setting up data center projects under shady shell companies or under the protection of nondisclosure agreements. She pointed to a tour stop in Jonesburg, Missouri, a small town in a county of 12,000 people. Google and Amazon have announced they will invest a combined $25 billion in data centers in the county over the coming years. “That is a David-versus-Goliath story,” she said. “How do you ever fight that alone?” The journey hasn’t been without its bumps. Kremer has received death threats, some from staunchly pro-AI people, her husband said. And sometimes the road has been too rough for the bus itself — one gravel road in Wakarusa, Kansas, proved impassable and forced the team to ask the owners of a nearby house whether they could hold their rally there instead of farther down the road. “Word got to the people down the dirt road, and then all of a sudden, before you know it, here they come,” Kremer said. “It was like ‘Field of Dreams.’ They just kept coming, the cars and the people. It just warms your heart.” The Humans First team is clear-eyed that not all Americans are completely on board with their message. President Donald Trump has repeatedly embraced data centers and the AI buildout as an economic boon that must be embraced, referring to AI as a “golden goose.” Kremer said she strongly disagrees with Trump about AI, pointing out that MAGA regulars don’t need to agree with him on every policy point. “He’s got a lot going on,” Kremer said, placing blame for misguided AI policy on the tech investors who use Trump’s attention to advance their anti-guardrail, pro-AI views. “I don’t want a data center in my backyard, and I don’t think President Trump wants a data center in his backyard, either,” she said. Several team members said they didn’t expect their tech-skeptical message to get a warm welcome from the tech companies themselves, either, though Kremer said she hadn’t tried too hard to get in touch with anyone at Anthropic, OpenAI or the other companies. “I’m just grateful to be able to help carry that message from city to city,” she said, looking back at the bus and its slogans. “People feel so isolated that it’s just happening to their town or community, and no one will pay attention.” Wrapping up the final interviews at the Anthropic stop, the gaggle of Humans First staff members boarded the bus as its diesel engine hummed back to life. Having completed its cross-country journey, the team said, the last mission was to drive over the Golden Gate Bridge to capture some final promotional video. “If the American people can stand together, it doesn’t matter how much money Big Tech has or how much they can control the algorithms,” Kylie Jane Kremer said. “There is nothing that can defeat the will of the American people.”

articles.title: He missed CSE at IIT Madras by 0.01 marks, got rejected at MIT; today he has a net worth of $20 billion: Meet Aravind Srinivas, the co-founder of Perplexity
articles.summary: Imagine missing your dream course by just 0.01. That is exactly what happened to Aravind Srinivas, a young student from Chennai.
articles.body: Imagine missing your dream course by just 0.01. That is exactly what happened to Aravind Srinivas, a young student from Chennai. After getting into IIT Madras for engineering, he tried to switch to another branch after his first semester, fell short of the cut-off by the tiniest margin, and felt another blow when he was rejected by MIT.Most people would have seen these as the end of the road. Srinivas saw them as motivation in a new direction and channelised his failure into success; today he is the co-founder of a renowned AI company and has a net worth of $2.1 billion, according to Forbes.Most success stories in the world do not follow a straight path, especially for those not born with a silver spoon in their mouth and those who carve out an identity for themselves.When doors of opportunity get closed in your face over and over again at the same time, it feels like the end of the road.Yet history is full of people who turned those moments into fuel, about how a detour from their planned route took them to immense heights of success, and this is one of those stories.Meet Aravind Srinivas: The co-founder of Perplexity who channelised his failures into successAravind Srinivas, 32, is the CEO and co-founder of Perplexity with Andy Konwinski, Denis Yarats, and Johnny Ho, which was valued at $20 billion in early 2026.Srinivas got into IIT Madras, where he studied electrical engineering, but after the first semester he wanted to switch his branch from electrical to computer science; however, it came as a blow when he missed the cut-off by just 0.01 and fell just short of the CGPA cut-off.“At the end of your first semester, IIT gives you an option to change your branch if you get about a certain CGPA (Cumulative Grade Point Average), and I missed that by 0.01. I thought that was the end of the world. I was so mad at myself,” he said in the Aarthi and Sriram podcast on YouTube.The setback pushed him to teach himself programming, describing how, he revealed, “I went into a whole shell. But that's when I discovered a lot of these online lectures, online competitive programming sites. I wasn't talking to anybody else; I was just like, absorbing myself and learning all these things myself, trying to solve all these problems. I started coding a lot. As a kid, it was more out of like vengeance – ‘let me prove the world wrong I'm actually good at this’. All that helped me later.He later interned with Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio, who recommended him for a PhD. Later again, even after being recommended, he faced disappointment, "MIT rejected me, Berkeley admitted me", he said.After Berkeley, he worked in top AI labs.Srinivas met research scientist John Schulman at the University of California, Berkeley, who was working with OpenAI then.“John Schulman, the guy who invented ChatGPT at OpenAI, he was also from Berkeley. He noticed my work, and he invited me to do an internship. So, that changed my life. I got into OpenAI,” Srinivas said.After his first internship at OpenAI, Srinivas spent the next couple of years, from around 2019 to 2021, working at DeepMind and Google. In 2021, he went back to OpenAI, led by Sam Altman. But he didn't stay long. About a year later, he decided to leave and start something of his own. In August 2022, he became the co-founder and CEO of Perplexity AI.Today, according to Forbes, Srinivas is worth $2.1 billion, placing him among India's youngest billionaires.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two
articles.summary: Nidal Malik Hasan killed 13 unarmed US soldiers and injured another 32 and his execution will be the first by the US military since 1961.
articles.body:
The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years.

Nidal Malik Hasan, a US Army major and physician, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.

It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.

Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder by a jury panel of 13 officers, which unanimously recommended his death sentence.

Parnell said the Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution.

"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X.

Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".

He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.

The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.

The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.

Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.

A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.

It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.

The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.

Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.

The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.

Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.

Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.

Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.

Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.

The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

articles.title: Separatist party wins Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity
articles.summary: The Parti Québécois, which secured a minority, has vowed to hold an independence referendum in the years to come.
articles.body:
Canadian media project the separatist Parti Québécois (PQ) will secure a minority win in Monday's provincial election in Quebec, making Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the incoming premier.

It marks the first time the PQ has been in power since 2014. It could prove to be a test for Prime Minister Mark Carney, setting up confrontations with Quebec over issues like immigration and the monarchy.

The party has also pledged to hold a referendum on Quebec's independence, similar to a process under way in the province of Alberta.

The majority French-speaking province has held other votes on this, in 1980 and 1995. Polls indicate only 30% of Quebecers back such a move.

Plamondon has said that vote would occur after US President Donald Trump is out of office.

Carney may find himself managing dual unity crises in different parts of the country, depending on the outcome of a vote in Alberta on whether to have a referendum.

Trump is due to leave office in roughly two years, meaning that if Plamondon keeps his pledge, a third vote on independence would likely be scheduled for 2029 or 2030.

Separate from sovereignty, Plamondon has made it clear he is willing to fight Ottawa if it is seen as overstepping matters of provincial interest.

He suggested during the campaign that he was going to pressure Ottawa on issues like immigration, vowing to fight any increases mandated by the Carney government.

He also pledged to "abolish the monarchy in Quebec" and reroute money spent on its institutions to social services instead.

"We are going to do what we have to do to get the monarchy out of Quebec, repatriate those funds, and send them to social causes," he told reporters in late September.

For example, Plamondon suggested defunding Quebec's lieutenant-governor's office - responsible for representing King Charles III in the province - saying he would instead spend that money to tackle homelessness.

Plamondon was among the Quebec lawmakers who refused to pledge allegiance to the King in 2022, paving the way for a provincial law that now makes the oath of allegiance optional.

His plan to withdraw financial support for the lieutenant-governor's office is likely to face significant legal challenges, given the monarchy's central role in Canada's constitution.

Such a move would also put future Quebec laws in doubt, as one of the key roles of the lieutenant-governor is to give royal assent to new legislation.

Pressed about these hurdles, Plamondon has told reporters that he is ready for a legal battle with the federal government.

The success of the Parti Québécois on Monday is in part due to public fatigue with the previous Coalition Avenir Québec government.

Coalition Avenir Québec made safeguarding Quebec's identity and language central to its eight years in office, but its longtime leader, François Legault, eventually lost significant support among voters.

Efforts to revive the party by replacing Legault with a new leader, outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette, were unsuccessful.

Fréchette conceded her own re-election race in Trois-Rivières shortly before 22:00 local time. She said in a speech that she would work with St-Pierre Plamondon on the transition.

"Governing Quebec is the greatest honour I have ever had," she said. "I have Quebec tattooed on my heart."

The Quebec Liberal Party secured the second-most seats, while the Quebec Conservative Party gained seats.

Prime Minister Carney, who leads the federal Liberal party, remains popular in Quebec, though support for him had recently dipped as US President Donald Trump imposed new tariffs on Canada in August, following a breakdown in trade talks.

Quebec is among the hardest hit by the latest US tariffs, with experts at global forecasting firm Oxford Economics projecting a C$2bn blow for the province.

Carney congratulated Plamondon on his victory late on Monday and vowed to work together with the party.

"Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada," he said in a post on social media. "I look forward to working with you to support Québec's businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec."

articles.title: Samoa leader apologises for Nazi salute after video from 2007 emerges
articles.summary: Schmidt acknowledged that his actions "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt".
articles.body:
Samoa's prime minister has apologised after a video emerged of him giving a Nazi salute while saying "Heil Hitler" at a family gathering.

In the seven-second clip filmed in July 2007, Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt is seen leading about a dozen people in the salute. "Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!" he says, then thanks the group for responding.

Schmidt has acknowledged that his words and gesture "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt", adding that the clip was recorded at a private gathering and "not intended for the public".

"I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism," Schmidt said in a statement published on Facebook on Monday.

The footage was first reported by local outlet the Samoa Observer in a news story on Sunday.

It said the video was filmed at a Schmidt family reunion in July 2007, when Schmidt was deputy speaker of parliament and quoted a family member who said he was the master of ceremonies at the gathering.

Samoa, a tiny island nation of about 221,000 people, sits about halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii.

It was under Germany's control in the early 20th century, but the colonisation ended shortly after World War One broke out.

Schmidt, who has Samoan and German heritage, took office as the country's eighth prime minister in September 2025.

He wore a Jewish prayer shawl during his swearing-in ceremony and has made clear his support for Israel during the early days of his premiership, saying that Samoa "stood with Israel".

"If people around the world don't like it, that's up to them, but Samoa stands with the land of God... There is only one God our country believes in, the God of Israel," he had said.

articles.title: Ron Thuma began saving his family’s heirloom seeds in the 1970s; decades later, he had shared more than 275 varieties with other gardeners
articles.summary: Ron Thuma began saving seeds from his family’s heirloom plants in the 1970s and went on to share more than 275 varieties through Seed Savers Exchange.
articles.body: Ron Thuma began saving seeds from his family’s heirloom plants in the 1970s and went on to share more than 275 varieties through Seed Savers Exchange. His collection grew after he joined John Withee’s Wanigan Associates. Thuma later learned about Seed Savers Exchange through an article in Organic Gardening magazine and began taking part in its work.According to Seed Savers Exchange, he has listed more than 275 varieties in the Exchange and stewarded even more in his own garden. Thuma became one of the organisation’s first Lifetime Members in 1984. After retiring, he continued gardening with his son, Josh, and kept detailed records of the varieties they grew and how they changed from season to season.How Ron Thuma turned family seeds into 275 varietiesRon Thuma first learned gardening from his father, and he began saving seeds in the 1970s. He started with a handful of Thuma family heirloom varieties and gradually expanded his collection. His interest grew after he joined John Withee’s Wanigan Associates.Thuma later discovered Seed Savers Exchange through an article in Organic Gardening magazine and began taking part in its work. Over the years, he listed more than 275 varieties in the Exchange while also caring for many more in his own garden.In 1984, he became one of Seed Savers Exchange’s first Lifetime Members. His seed work continued alongside his job in Kansas, as he shared the varieties he grew with other gardeners through the Exchange.Why has Thuma’s garden become a local tradition in HartfordGardening remained closely tied to Thuma’s family life. After retiring, he continues to pass on his love of gardening to his grandchildren. One of the family’s favourites is the ‘Apple’ pepper, which Thuma first acquired in the early 1990s as a trial variety sent to loyal customers by Johnny’s Selected Seeds of Maine.The pepper became a Thuma family favourite, and both Ron and Josh still grow it in their gardens. Josh said his two-year-old daughter enjoys the sweet peppers and eats them whole like an apple. Thuma’s garden has also become a part of Hartford, Kansas. Jack Bohannan, a project leader at the wildlife refuge, described the garden as a local legend and said Thuma still works in it.How has Thuma tracked his varieties over the yearsThuma and his son, Josh, keep detailed records of the varieties they grow in their garden. During each growing season, Thuma notes the yield, plant performance, weather, and harvest dates in a working notebook. Once the season ends, he transfers the information to an archival binder. He also keeps a card file with separate notes for each variety. The 3-by-5-inch index cards record the purity and characteristics of each variety from one year to the next.Together, the records provide a nearly 30-year account of Thuma’s gardening successes and failures. They also document the plants he continues to grow and steward. This careful record-keeping allows Thuma to track individual varieties over many years and keep a detailed history of his work with them.Thuma combined gardening with community serviceThuma’s gardening work is part of a wider life of service in Hartford and at the Flint Hills National Wildlife Refuge. He taught in a small Kansas public school before spending 36 years as a maintenance supervisor at the refuge.There, he worked in many roles and placed a strong emphasis on teaching young people. He implemented the Youth Conservation Corps programme, which gave high school students summer employment through projects including trail building and invasive plant control.Thuma also served as a volunteer firefighter in Hartford for 35 years and as the city’s mayor. articles.title: Secessionist party wins Quebec election in Canada
articles.summary: Parti Quebecois returns to power, promising a third referendum on Quebec’s independence from Canada.
articles.body:
The secessionist Parti Quebecois has won the most seats in Quebec’s election and will form the next government in the predominantly French-speaking Canadian province, according to media reports.

The result on Monday revives the question of whether the province should leave Canada, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s message of national unity.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the party’s leader, is set to become premier.

During the campaign, he promised a third referendum on leaving Canada during his first term, although he said he would wait until US President Donald Trump leaves office in January 2029.

It was not yet clear whether the party had reached the 64 seats needed for a majority in the 127-seat National Assembly.

If it falls short, it would lead a minority government and need support from opposition lawmakers to pass major legislation and survive confidence votes.

The Parti Quebecois, or PQ, last governed the province from 2012 to 2014.

Monday’s victory marks a sharp recovery for the PQ, which won just three seats in the 2022 provincial election.

Its return also ends eight years in power for the Coalition Avenir Quebec, or CAQ, a centre-right Quebec nationalist party that does not support independence.

Daniel Beland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal, told The Associated Press news agency that the victory reflects Quebec’s multiparty system, where support is divided among several parties, rather than a surge in secessionist sentiment.

Support for independence remains at about 30 percent, low by historical standards, he said.

Still, Beland said a secessionist government in Quebec represents a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching in Alberta.

“Seeing that a pro-independence party won in Quebec barely two weeks before an independence-related referendum takes place in Alberta might suggest to the Trump administration that national unity remains a major issue in Canada despite the popularity of Mark Carney,” Beland said.

Quebec held two previous referendums on independence, in 1980 and 1995, and voters rejected secession both times.

The second vote was decided by a narrow margin, but there has been no further referendum in the three decades since.

articles.title: Nepal ends search and rescue after deadly flood, with more than 5,200 still missing
articles.summary: Authorities say they need nearly $5 billion to help the thousands of people displaced by the Aug. 26 flood originating at Nepal’s border with China’s Tibet region.
articles.body: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Nepal has ended the search and rescue operation for those still missing after the devastating flood in August that killed at least 1,455 people, officials said Monday. At least 5,285 people were still missing after the Aug. 26 flood originating at Nepal’s border with China’s Tibet region. An additional 13,795 people were rescued. “We are moving from the search and rescue phase to the search and rehabilitation phase,” Phanindra Paudel, chief of the National Emergency Operation Center, told Reuters. He said authorities were considering how to legally declare the missing people dead to allow their families or relatives to complete insurance, banking and other legal formalities. “We are initiating due processes to complete required legal formalities,” Paudel said. Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said authorities would no longer actively search for bodies but would recover any remains, property or other valuables found during the rehabilitation process. Uprety said emergency rescues would still be carried out if needed. The flood also destroyed 12 hydroelectric projects, roads, bridges, farms and settlements. Authorities have said they need nearly $5 billion for the early recovery and rehabilitation of the thousands of people displaced by the flood.

articles.title: South Korea blames North Korean mines for border blast injuries and demands apology
articles.summary: North Korea has denied responsibility for the Sept. 21 blasts and threatened “merciless” retaliation if it’s provoked over the case.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea’s military said Monday it concluded North Korea planted mines that injured three South Korean soldiers at their heavily fortified border last month, urging the North to apologize and remove other mines. The announcement came days after North Korea denied responsibility for the Sept. 21 blasts and threatened “merciless” retaliation if provoked over the case. It followed South Korea’s earlier, preliminary finding that said there was a “very high possibility” that mines buried by North Korea caused the explosions. On Monday, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it reached a final conclusion that North Korean mines planted just south of the border exploded and injured the three soldiers who were working on creating a patrol route in a densely vegetated area. It cited a joint investigation of the site with the American-led U.N. Command, forensic analysis of TNT and other substances collected from the South Korean soldiers’ uniforms and one other North Korean mine discovered days after the blast. “Our military strongly urges North Korea to offer a sincere apology to our injured soldiers and immediately remove the mines that it installed in violation of an armistice agreement” that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War, Lt. Gen. Kwon Dae-won, vice chairman of South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, told a televised briefing. The armistice agreement prohibits both sides from committing any hostile act “within, from, or against” the Demilitarized Zone, a border buffer zone, and bans military or civilian personnel from crossing the military demarcation line without authorization from the armistice commission. Despite its name, the DMZ is one of the world’s most heavily armed border areas, with an estimated 2 million mines littered inside and along the zone. North Korea in recent years has added mines, barbed wire fences, anti-tank barriers and other front-line fortifications along the border, as leader Kim Jong Un declared South Korea his country’s main enemy. South Korea’s military said North Korean soldiers violated the border’s military demarcation line 17 times last year and 50 times this year during their border fortification works. South Korea responded by firing warning shots. In November 2025, South Korea proposed talks on clarifying the borderline, but North Korea did not respond. Kwon said the South Korean military removed a North Korean minefield around the blast site on Monday and will remove other North Korean minefields placed south of the border unless North Korea voluntarily eliminates them. South Korea’s military earlier said it would take unspecified corresponding steps against North Korea if the North is conclusively found responsible for the mine blasts. But South Korea did not immediately announce any substantial punitive steps on Monday. In 2015, mine blasts at the border blamed on North Korea pushed the two Koreas to the brink of an armed conflict, after South Korea’s then-conservative government resumed front-line propaganda broadcasts for the first time in 11 years. Kim’s sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, last week called the preliminary South Korean assessment on the blasts a “conspiratorial farce” and vowed to take “immediate and merciless retaliatory action” if South Korea opens fire at North Korean soldiers fortifying the border. The latest mine explosions came at a delicate time when South Korea’s liberal government is making efforts to coordinate a resumption of talks between North Korea and the U.S., hoping that would help restart its own talks with the North and promote peace on the Korean Peninsula. North Korea has been shunning all forms of dialogue with South Korea and the U.S. since Kim Jong Un’s high-stakes nuclear diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump fell apart in 2019. North Korea said Saturday it test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile that it claimed cannot be intercepted because of its low-altitude maneuverability and artificial intelligence capabilities. South Korea’s Defense Ministry responded that the South Korean and U.S. militaries are capable of intercepting that missile.

articles.title: New York declares disaster emergency over measles, 108 cases reported
articles.summary: New York state has declared a disaster emergency over a rise in measles cases, as the disease continues to spread across parts of the United States.
articles.body: New York state has declared a disaster emergency over a rise in measles cases, as the disease continues to spread across parts of the United States.Governor Kathy Hochul said the emergency declaration would expand the pool of health professionals who can administer measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines and allow more healthcare workers to order testing.The declaration will remain in effect through November 4.108 cases reported in New YorkNew York has recorded 108 measles cases this year as of October 3, including seven in New York City and 101 elsewhere in the state.Hochul said 92 of the cases recorded since July 15 were in under-immunised rural communities across 18 counties.Local health departments have administered more than 1,000 MMR vaccine doses across rural parts of the state since July 15, according to the state health department.“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” Hochul said, adding that the emergency measures would help increase access to vaccination and testing.The executive order allows paramedics, advanced EMS providers, pharmacists and midwives to administer measles vaccines. Nurses will also be allowed to order testing.US measles cases continue to climbThe emergency declaration comes as measles cases rise across the US. Pennsylvania has reported more than 1,000 cases this year, while outbreaks have also been recorded in Texas, Utah, Ohio and South Carolina.Health experts have linked the resurgence to vaccination rates falling below the 95% level considered necessary to prevent outbreaks.The US had eliminated domestic transmission of measles in 2000. The last outbreak involving more than 1,000 cases occurred over several years in New York City in the early 1990s.International health officials are due to meet in November to determine whether the US and Mexico will retain their measles-free status.The Pan American Health Organisation has stressed the need for high and consistent vaccination coverage, stronger disease surveillance and a rapid response to outbreaks.State expands vaccination effortsNew York's health department said it was working with local authorities to track cases, conduct contact tracing and speed up laboratory testing.The state has also launched a measles dashboard to help residents and healthcare officials track local risks.The health department urged New Yorkers to check their MMR vaccination status, particularly before travelling to areas experiencing outbreaks.It said one MMR dose provides 93% protection against measles, while two doses provide 97% protection.Measles is highly contagious and can cause serious complications including pneumonia, brain swelling and death. The disease spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.The state health department urged people who develop symptoms to contact healthcare providers before visiting a clinic or hospital so that infection-control measures can be taken.You use AI every day. articles.title: 2 workers injured, 500 evacuated after massive fire guts labour camp outside Lucknow airport; watch
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: At least two workers were injured while evacuating a three-storey makeshift labour camp after a major fire engulfed the structure outside
articles.body: LUCKNOW: At least two workers were injured while evacuating a three-storey makeshift labour camp after a major fire engulfed the structure outside Chaudhary Charan Singh International Airport on Tuesday morning.The blaze broke out around 6.50am at the Tata Projects labour colony, about 800 metres from the airport. The PVC-panel structure housed workers engaged in ongoing airport development projects. Thick smoke and flames were visible from several kilometres away, triggering panic in the area.The injured workers were identified as Nirmal, 30, son of Mukhiya, a resident of Saharsa in Bihar, and Rahul Kumar, 26, son of Bhagwati Din Pal, a resident of Salipur in Pratapgarh. Both were taken for medical attention. The Fire Department said neither had sustained burn injuries.The camp had 33 rooms, with 11 on each floor, and could accommodate around 500 workers deployed in round-the-clock shifts. The fire spread rapidly through the combustible panels and engulfed the structure within minutes. Officials did not specify how many workers were present when the fire broke out.The Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting team immediately dispatched a Domestic Fire Tender to the site, while a Crash Fire Tender from the airport and fire tenders from the Uttar Pradesh Fire Service were also deployed. All workers were evacuated safely, officials said.A newly introduced 22,000-litre water bowser was among the fire tenders deployed by the UP Fire Service headquarters. Firefighters climbed to the first and second floors to tackle the flames from close quarters. Two LPG cylinders exploded during the operation, increasing the risk to the firefighting teams.The blaze was brought under control in about 45 minutes and was prevented from spreading to nearby areas. Chief Fire Officer Ankush Mittal reached the site and supervised the operation.An inspection later indicated that the fire started in Barrack 9 while food was being prepared. The temporary structure was completely damaged.“Initial findings shared by Tata Projects indicate that the fire started while some labourers were preparing food using LPG cylinders. The company provides meals for its workers, and the use of flammable materials or unauthorised cooking arrangements within the labour colony is prohibited. articles.title: Jim Bakker, whose globe-spanning PTL ministry fell to scandal and fraud, dies at 86
articles.summary: Jim Bakker, the charismatic evangelical preacher who built a Christian television empire, only to see it collapse in scandal, recrimination and prison, died Monday, his wife said.
articles.body: Jim Bakker, the charismatic evangelical preacher who built a Christian television empire, only to see it collapse in scandal, recrimination and prison, died Monday, his wife said. He was 86. “It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” his second wife, Lori Bakker, said on the Facebook page of Bakker’s most recent TV show, “The Jim Bakker Show.” She did not disclose a cause of death. Bakker’s son, Jay Bakker, who became a prominent evangelist in his own right with a much more liberal view of Christianity than his father’s, confirmed the death in his own Facebook post. “We had a very complicated relationship and he was also my father and a grandfather and I need to mourn in my own time,” he wrote. Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and his flamboyant first wife, Tammy Faye, was born in International Falls, Minnesota, but they embraced the South when they started a puppet show on a Virginia TV station in the 1970s. It soon turned into a high-energy, Southern-flavored talk show called “The PTL Club” on cable, attracting some of the biggest celebrities of the 1980s to tell their stories of having been “born again.” Bakker launched the first Christian satellite network to beam his upbeat message — “God loves you. He really does” — into homes across the country and around the world. Along the way, the Bakkers became known in the secular world for their easy tears, Jim Bakker’s welcoming but often strict message and Tammy Bakker’s neon personality — and makeup. Their ministry grew rapidly, and operating out of its new base in Fort Mill, South Carolina, along the North Carolina line, they built a multimillion-dollar empire complete with one of the world’s largest theme parks, Heritage USA, on the small donations of hundreds of thousands of believers, some of whom pledged their life savings to them. But PTL — short, variously, for Praise the Lord or People That Love — collapsed in 1987, when The Charlotte Observer reported that PTL had paid more than $250,000 to Jessica Hahn, a church secretary with whom he had a one-time tryst years earlier. Bakker confirmed the encounter to the Observer but said he had been “wickedly manipulated by treacherous former friends and then colleagues who victimized me with the aid of a female confederate.” Further reporting disclosed lavish spending on the Bakkers’ behalf, including an air-conditioned doghouse at their lakefront home and gold-plated bathroom fixtures. The Bakkers resigned from PTL, and in 1989, Bakker was convicted of fraud and conspiracy and sentenced to 45 years in prison; he served just less than five years before he was paroled. Tammy Bakker resolutely stood by him for several years, but in 1992 she filed for divorce. She married the man whose contracting service built much of Heritage USA — and who provided most of the money to pay Hahn — and slowly rebuilt her life as a Christian TV personality who knowingly winked at her own image for secular audiences. She died of cancer in 2007. Jim Bakker returned to ministry after his prison term and in 2003 launched “The Jim Bakker Show” with Lori Bakker, whom he had married in 1998. Bakker’s message was far different this time — apocalyptic and dismissive of the prosperity theology that brought him to fame. The show focused on a survivalist message, and Bakker built a new business based on promoting unregulated supplements. In 2021, he and his church settled a lawsuit from the state of Missouri that accused him of falsely claiming a health supplement called Silver Solution could cure Covid. “He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” Lori Bakker said Monday night in announcing his death.

articles.title: 'More skeletons are tumbling out': Congress trains guns at EC over new report on Bengal polls
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh on Tuesday accused the Election Commission of overseeing \"mass manipulation
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh on Tuesday accused the Election Commission of overseeing "mass manipulation and rigging" during the West Bengal assembly polls. He further demanded accountability from Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as well as other two election commissioners along with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and home minister Amit Shah."More skeletons are tumbling out of the Election Omission of India’s closet. Clearly the PM-HM strategy was to somehow capture and win the West Bengal Assembly elections at any cost. It was a text book case of mass manipulation and rigging which was overseen by the CEC. The puppet has of course to go but the two puppeteers too have to be held accountable. They stand brutally exposed and now it is only a matter of time for them to meet their reckoning," Ramesh wrote in a post on X."Today, MPs of the INDIA janbandhan plus other Opposition MPs who have also been invited will be marching peacefully to the Election Commission of India to demand the CEC's resignation. Looks like the Parliament complex is already under an unprecedented security siege showing the extreme nervousness of the puppeteer pair," he added.Ramesh's remarks followed a media report claiming that judges of more than a dozen tribunals appointed in West Bengal on the Supreme Court's directions to hear appeals related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), including those involving 27 lakh deleted electors, had flagged gaps in a digital portal created by the Election Commission's IT division.The Congress has stepped up its criticism of the poll panel amid a wider dispute over the SIR exercise. The opposition's latest attack also comes after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modification to Form 6, the application used by eligible voters to seek inclusion in electoral rolls.A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said, "We will examine all the decisions. If any decision is not in accordance with the law, we will annul it. You know the power of the court."The bench also said, "any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When records are produced, we would like to see who has modified it".The Congress and other opposition parties have demanded Kumar's resignation, alleging that changes to Form 6 were made unilaterally during the SIR process. Rahul Gandhi on Monday said the CEC and others involved in what he called a "criminal assault on democracy" would be held accountable.Separately, a report by The Indian Express said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders, many concerning the SIR exercise.The Election Commission has rejected concerns arising from the reported differences, saying divergent views are part of institutional deliberations and that its orders have full legal sanction and follow established statutory procedures.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2011, California completed a 300-acre restoration of former San Diego salt ponds; five-year monitoring later documented 80 bird, 22 fish and 10 invertebrate species
articles.summary: For decades, parts of South San Diego Bay looked very different from the tidal wetlands that once occupied them.
articles.body: For decades, parts of South San Diego Bay looked very different from the tidal wetlands that once occupied them. Former salt ponds had been separated from the bay, limiting natural tidal flows and reducing habitat for wildlife. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the Southern California Wetlands Recovery Project, a partnership involving federal, state and local agencies and conservation groups began restoring the landscape in the late 2000s. By 2011, roughly 300 acres across the western salt ponds, the Chula Vista Wildlife Reserve and Emory Cove had been restored. The work included reshaping degraded areas, creating tidal channels, breaching levees to restore tidal influence and establishing native plant communities.Bringing the tides backSome of the western salt ponds had been cut off from tidal influence since around 1960 or earlier. During restoration, sediment was moved to create a network of channels and the existing levees were breached, allowing water from the bay and the Otay River channel to flow into the restored areas.The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says the project ultimately transformed the former salt ponds into a combination of open water, intertidal habitat and upland marsh. The restoration was completed in 2011, with planting, maintenance and ecological monitoring continuing for five years afterward. The result was not simply a wetter landscape. It became habitat.Wildlife began returningThe most striking evidence came from the post-construction monitoring programme. Over five years, researchers documented 80 species of birds, 22 species of fish and 10 species of invertebrates using the restored site.Birds were among the most visible beneficiaries. The restored wetlands provided feeding and foraging areas for migratory and resident species, while newly established marsh vegetation created habitat for species of conservation concern.The Southern California Wetlands Recovery Project says more than 90 species of migratory and residential birds are currently benefiting from the broader restoration area. Among them are the California least tern, light-footed Ridgway’s rail, western snowy plover and Belding’s savannah sparrow. The return of fish was equally significant. Reconnected tidal channels created shallow-water areas that could serve as feeding and spawning habitat, strengthening the ecological value of the bay.A wetland begins to rebuild itselfOne of the clearest signs of recovery came surprisingly quickly. Native plants began appearing within less than a year of the restoration, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service.Researchers also found that the restored site was developing into nursery habitat for fish and invertebrates. Monitoring conducted after construction found natural recruitment of native vegetation, including eelgrass, which is an important food source for eastern Pacific green sea turtles. The project also helped create habitat for the endangered light-footed Ridgway’s rail, one of the restoration effort’s key targets. By 2016, the Fish and Wildlife Service reported successful breeding at the restored site.From salt ponds to living wetlandsThe restoration was part of a wider effort to recover coastal habitats that had been heavily altered by development, dredging and filling around San Diego Bay. Historical losses had left only a fraction of the bay’s original intertidal and salt-marsh habitat intact.Today, the restored landscape also offers people a chance to see the ecological changes firsthand through the Bayside Birding and Walking Trail, where visitors can observe birds using the marsh.What was once a landscape dominated by former industrial salt ponds has consequently become a functioning piece of the coastal ecosystem again. And the five-year monitoring results provide a measurable record of that change: 80 bird species, 22 fish species and 10 invertebrate species using habitat that had once been largely cut off from the tides.You use AI every day. articles.title: Community supermarket opens in Chatham shopping centre
articles.summary: Shoppers can access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries at the new social supermarket.
articles.body:
A new community supermarket offering access to affordable and healthy food has opened in a Kent shopping centre.

The store run by SEK Community Food Shop welcomed the public to its home on the first floor of The Pentagon Centre in Chatham.

Gina English from SEK says the shop is open to all as "in addition to supporting people with food insecurity, people will also be able get wraparound support from us, help with employment, looking at CVs and interview skills. We're also going to help people with budgeting and money management and signposting to other local services".

Initial funding to set up the supermarket was provided by Medway Council through the Crisis and Resilience Fund.

Shoppers can walk straight into the social supermarket, with no prior booking required, to access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries, including a £1 fruit and vegetable bag.

Cost are kept low as the store redistributes surplus food to reduce waste, helping to protect the environment at the same time.

SEK already operates two similar stores in Kent.

English said: "We've had Ramsgate for about three years, Ashford just for just over a year and across the two shops in the last year alone we saw 55,500 transactions and we were able to save 170 tonnes of perfectly good food from going to waste, so they do work."

Some of the first to experienced the store were Shirley Graves and her partner Rod Taffs who have already filled their basket with bargains.

"People want to come down and see what they've got, it's amazing," says Graves.

"I've got a box of 20 samosas for £1.50 and a big huge bag of chicken for £6. Times are quite tight at the moment, being pensioners, it's cheap and the chicken is amazing."

"That's going to do us three or four meals," adds Taffs.

Medway Council leader, Vince Maple, said: "I think most people across Kent and Medway would want to see food not going to waste, so the ability to have good quality food at a reasonable price, helping not just our families and individuals on low incomes but helping all families has got to be a good thing."

The shop also has a confidential, soundproofed office pod at the back of the store where customers can seek personal advice and guidance.

The SEK Community Food Shop in The Pentagon Centre, Chatham, is open Monday to Saturday between 10:00 and 18:00.
