articles.title: Rise in babies in care proceedings raises fears of unnecessary adoptions, experts tell BBC
articles.summary: With better support, many babies may not have needed to go into care, File on 4 Investigates is told.
articles.body:
The number of children involved in care proceedings before they reach their first birthdays is at a persistently high level across England, according to experts who have published new figures.

Data from the universities of Lancaster and Oxford indicates care proceedings for babies have risen by 64% over the past two decades, with one in 118 infants affected. The figures - up to 2024-25 - peaked during Covid, before dropping slightly and plateauing.

While there are cases where it is unsafe for parents to continue contact with their children, experts have told File on 4 Investigates that many babies may not have needed to go into care if support had been in place.

And, since very young children who go into care are more likely to be adopted than older children, there are also concerns from experts that some may have been permanently separated from their birth families unnecessarily.

The BBC understands that new guidance for Family Court judges, to significantly reduce the number of short-notice care hearings - within hours or days of a baby being born - will be announced before the end of the year.

According to latest government figures, 72% of adopted children in England went into care before turning one.

Most of the adoptions, more than 90%, went ahead without parents' written consent - according to CoramBAAF, which represents those working in adoption and care.

Courts overruled parents' wishes in just under half of those cases. The rest were classed as "unopposed", with many parents advised not to contest the adoptions, because they would be unlikely to succeed.

Adoption should be pursued as a last resort, the government and adoption organisations have told us, because, while it offers stability, it also severs the legal relationship between the child and its birth family forever.

When a child is placed in care, birth parents are often allowed contact - but not always.

Analysis of care proceedings suggests between a fifth and a quarter were "clear-cut", where a child had suffered serious harm or abuse, says Prof Karen Broadhurst from Lancaster University.

But the majority were "grey area" cases of neglect by families with complex needs, she says, including drug and alcohol abuse, and housing issues, which might have improved with support.

However, children's charity Coram - which, like CoramBAAF, is part of a wider network of specialist children's organisations - warns that if infants in care are not adopted, they would likely remain in care. And research shows that many children brought up in the care system experience much poorer outcomes in life than those outside it.

Social workers are at the heart of the decision-making process as to whether a child should be taken into care.

One of them, whom we are calling Tracy, describes the dilemmas she and her colleagues face daily, balancing giving families time to get through a crisis, against the risk of failing to intervene.

She says she and her colleagues carry out wide-ranging and detailed assessments of parents - including judging whether there is enough past and present evidence of a future risk of harm to their children.

In some cases, she says, they deal with families "riddled with abuse and neglect" where no-one is able to safely bring up a child.

The stakes could not be higher. Extreme, high-profile cases, like those of Baby P in north London and Sara Sharif in Woking, Surrey, have served as a reminder of that.

The British Association of Social Workers told us their members are doing their best against a backdrop of increasing caseloads and reduction in resources.

With only about 10% of adoptions in England made with written consent from birth parents, according to CoramBAAF, this has led campaigners and some experts to describe the situation as modern-day "forced adoption".

Broadhurst acknowledges that term is "politically loaded" and the modern care system is very different from the coercive practices that took place mainly between 1949 and 1976 - and for which the government recently apologised for cases in England.

But she says it "is actually what's happening because parents do not agree".

"They want to continue to be in contact with a child," she says. "Even parents who feel they couldn't look after a child at that point find it particularly brutal that they're going to have no contact, or very little contact, with that child until they're 18."

One birth mother, Jean, tells us she never wanted to give up her daughter, Tye, for adoption - and describes it as "forced". Her local council says it followed a lawful process.

Jean was separated from her daughter for 16 years, after Tye was taken into care at 11 weeks' old and then adopted at the age of two.

Now, with Tye an adult, they are reunited. When she turned 18, having struggled with adoption and questions about her identity, Tye looked for her mother on social media.

"I knew I had a mum somewhere and it wasn't the people I was growing up with," she says - describing her adoption as something that had left her "completely alone" without a "whole chunk of heritage".

When Jean became pregnant, she was looking forward to being a mother. But she had concerns too: "The only thing I knew for certain was that I was disabled, I couldn't look after myself properly, so I wasn't sure how I was going to be able to look after a baby, so I needed help."

Her local authority at the time, Newham Council in east London, told her such help was not available, she says. Tye was put into foster care, but Jean was able to see her often.

There had been multiple assessments and residential placements as Jean tried to keep Tye. But professionals, including doctors and social workers, ultimately advised the court that Tye needed a stable, permanent family and that Jean could not provide it.

Jean says she fought and "gave it my all" through years of court proceedings. She even asked if she could have visiting rights, in a similar way to a parent in a divorce. "I was told that was an unrealistic expectation," she says.

Newham Council told the BBC Jean had been offered "extensive support", including 24-hour-a-day help in a residential mother and baby unit.

It said Jean had been offered contact with Tye through "two-way letterbox communication" - when birth parents and adoptive parents send letters or emails to each other - which was "a standard way for birth parents to remain in contact with children who have been adopted".

Sarah Johal - who heads Adoption England, which works with adoption agencies - says she understands why some birth parents might use the term "forced adoption". But today's decisions are "a response to child protection", she says, with the Family Court considering all the options for each child.

Although birth parents lose all legal responsibility for their children post-adoption, Johal says there is a chance for emails and photos to be exchanged: "We've really been trying to advocate for the need for more support for birth families around helping with contact."

Since Tye's adoption, support for birth families across England has been reduced.

Spending on early intervention services has been cut by 44% over a decade, according to a report commissioned by the Children's Services Funding Alliance. The costs of looking after children in care have risen by 50% in the same period.

With less funding for local authorities, it has been hard to help struggling parents cope, says social worker, Tracy.

Had a family been given better support at the beginning of care proceedings, she says, "maybe the child wouldn't have needed to be removed… maybe the child wouldn't have needed to be adopted."

Lancaster University's Karen Broadhurst says the reduction in support means that more of the "grey area" cases happen.

"In the face of cutbacks in preventative services and huge waiting lists, what's happening is those grey cases, those borderline cases, more of those children are coming to care," Broadhurst explains.

Concern has also grown that an increasing number of care decisions are made too quickly.

More than half of urgent care hearings in England in 2024-25 were for newborns, where mothers had to attend court within days of giving birth or even potentially on the same day.

The new guidance for judges, the BBC understands, will allow family courts to be "rigorous in refusing to deal with cases that do not meet the criteria of urgency".

But Broadhurst, who sat on the working group for the new guidance, says judges are just one "cog in the chain" of a wider system of support and intervention for families in crisis.

"If a case comes in on a Friday afternoon, what are they [judges] going to do? What resources do they have at their fingertips to say no?" she says. "So I think they're in a really unenviable position."

The government is investing £2.4bn to transform children's social care - including giving children and their families earlier and better support, to help them stay together wherever possible - a Department for Education spokesperson told us.

Research from the Nuffield Family Justice Observatory (NFJO) consistently shows that providing early, intensive support to birth mothers - especially those facing repeat care proceedings - is critical to safely reducing the number of children entering the care system.

In Salford, the work of one project suggests that, with the right support, many children in "grey area" cases can stay out of care.

Strengthening Families works with parents, most of whom have previously had a child removed, and offers specialised, intensive support during a child's early years. About three-quarters of families referred have been able to stay together, staff told us.

Some parents had "quite awful experiences in their life", team member Jude Hannam says, but "that can lead them to be an even better parent, because they don't want to parent how they were".

There are still cases where children still need to be removed from birth parents. The project's dedicated midwife, Adele Martin - having built up trust with pregnant mothers - is the one who has to step in.

"It's probably the most important bit of my job I think. And a mum who's in utter crisis says, 'yeah, you can take my baby from my arms'. That's really something," she says emotionally.

articles.title: Birmingham gallery celebrates city's people, places and sounds
articles.summary: A new gallery tells the story of the city through the eyes of Birmingham Museums' Citizens' Jury.
articles.body:
A new gallery celebrating the people, places, sounds and experiences that have shaped Birmingham since the 1950s is opening at Birmingham Museum & Art Gallery.

A City That Can opens on Tuesday, and tells the story of the city through the eyes of Birmingham Museums' Citizens' Jury.

The jury was commissioned by Birmingham Museums Trust in 2024 to challenge ideas about who museums are for and what belongs in them. The exhibition focuses not just on famous people and historic events, but on everyday lives, memories and experiences.

It explores some of the jury's recommendations through three themes: Be Loud, Make Change and Play Hard.

Birmingham Museums Trust co-chief executives, Sara Wajid and Zak Mensah, said the gallery celebrates the stories of people across the city.

They added: "Rather than presenting a single version of Birmingham's history, the new gallery invites visitors to explore the extraordinary stories of ordinary Brummies and to consider how their own experiences fit into the city's ever-changing story."

Discarded lamp-post flags turned into 'unity' artwork

The 'prince of pop art who was forgotten by his home' city finally gets exhibition

The first theme, Be Loud, focuses on Birmingham's activism, community spirit and musical heritage, organisers said.

Objects include a 1950s portable record player, an Honor melodeon donated by Irish musician, Pat Brennan, and material connected to Birmingham-based Oriental Star Agencies record label.

There are also 1962 membership cards for the Tudor Dance & Social Club at the Locarno dance hall in Hurst Street.

The gallery explores the communities and businesses that helped shape the city, including its curry house history.

A recreated table setting from the Koh-I-Noor curry house recalls one of Birmingham's earliest curry houses, which opened on Horse Fair in the 1960s.

Artist and curator, Mohammed Ali, saved parts of the restaurant including original partitions and unused rolls of wallpaper, when the building was being renovated.

The Play Hard section looks at Birmingham's sporting history, with objects including boots and a mouthguard donated by Birmingham-born bare-knuckle boxer, Melanie Shah, skates belonging to speed skater, Eric Grinsell, and a Small Heath Harriers running shirt.

It also features Chad Valley toys made in Birmingham between the 1950s and 1970s, and a vintage Cluedo game.

Cluedo was invented in Birmingham during the Second World War by Anthony Pratt. His wife, Elva, also helped design the board.

The Make Change element tells the story of the Citizens' Jury in the jurors' own words and explores the impact of their work.

The Citizens' Jury was the first of its kind to take place in a UK museum.

It was supported by the National Lottery Heritage Fund and facilitated by Shared Future.

Wajid and Mensah added: "We hope visitors will help us build on Birmingham's story by sharing their own memories, knowledge and experiences. Museums don't have to be the final word on history – they can be places where stories continue to grow."

articles.title: York city walls 'tap to donate' scheme raises nearly £9,000
articles.summary: One donor gave £400 for the upkeep of York's city walls during the first year of the pilot scheme.
articles.body:
A trial scheme raising money towards the conservation of York's city walls has raised nearly £9,000 in its first year, figures reveal.

'Tap to donate' points, installed at Bootham Bar last September at a cost of £10,000, allow users to give money towards stonemasonry maintenance works.

According to council figures obtained through a freedom of information request by the Local Democracy Reporting Service , £8,136 has been raised via donation points and £530 has been donated online.

One generous donor gave £400 towards the walls, with the single donation the largest offered during the first year of the scheme.

The contactless donation points allow people to donate £3, £5 and £10 and were installed along with QR codes for custom donations and wall information boards.

Speaking at its launch last year, City of York Council officials said it can cost £600,000 a year to maintain the walls.

If 5% of the city's 2.5 million annual visitors paid £5, the expense would be covered, the authority added.

July was the most lucrative month for donations with £1,295 raised, with the lowest in January raising £105.

Liam Dennis, the local authority's ancient monuments lead, said: "Some of the donations were very kind.

"Any amount of money is gratefully received and it goes directly towards the conservation of the walls and shows how important they are to visitors and the people of York."

He continued: "Bootham Bar was the easiest location to start with because it's under cover and already has plug sockets.

"We're now examining other locations, but each has its own challenges."

Paul Roberts, who used the contactless donation point at Bootham Bar, said he thought it was a good idea at first glance, with others positive about the scheme.

"I hope that people will donate if they are in a position to," said Samantha Nash, from St Albans.

"The council have a certain responsibility to do what they can to maintain these things rather than leave it to the public to do."

Councillor Pete Kilbane, the council's executive member for economy and culture, hoped the scheme would be expanded to further sections of the wall.

"Somebody might walk past this donation point, walk round the walls and think, 'this is fantastic, I should have given a fiver to that'.

"If there is another point that they can do that then we think it will work out better."

York was first fortified with walls in Roman times, though very little of the remaining stonework survives from that period.

Most of the walls standing today date from the 13th and 14th Century.

They are the longest surviving town walls in England, running for more than two miles (3.4km).

articles.title: Frome Birth Talk: 'Life-saving' charity for new mums might have to close support
articles.summary: The charity recently lost out on a bid for funding and now might have to close its waiting list.
articles.body:
A "life-saving" charity that supports new mothers may have to close its waiting list if urgent funding cannot be raised.

Frome Birth Talk provided counselling to more than 155 mothers in 2026, but charity chiefs warn they will have to cut back on support unless they can raise £10,000 by Sunday.

Sarah N'Guio received counselling from the charity a year after giving birth and said it saved her life, adding: "Without them, I probably would have lost my children and lost my life."

Suzy Cristinacce, charity director, said: "More and more people are suffering from mental health problems and the charity sector is helping fill the gaps but the pot is getting smaller and smaller."

Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86

Bridge replacement delayed due to summer heatwaves

'Devious' scout leader jailed over child sex abuse

After a traumatic birth where she nearly died, N'Guio's mental health plummeted.

"I was spiralling, had imposter syndrome, postpartum depression and constantly felt under attack,"she told BBC Radio Somerset.

"I felt people were plotting against me and that was when I decided to ask for help.

"The charity held me, allowed me to let go of my worries and fears and gave me space to make sense of things," she said.

The Royal College of Midwives reports that about one in four new mums will face a mental health issue after giving birth.

Cristinacce said about 50% of the charity's money is generated from grant funding.

"I don't know what has happened, but I'm applying for grants, the feedback is that our application is very strong but the grants aren't coming in," Cristinacce said.

She added that they have set up a crowdfunding site that will be open until Sunday.

A spokesperson for the Royal United Hospitals (RUH) Bath said other support is available for women in the area.

They also said an NHS pathway includes a referral into the RUH perinatal mental health team.

NHS England has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Banks still refusing credit cards in Jersey, watchdog says
articles.summary: Applications are being denied despite a change to make it easier, Jersey Consumer Council says.
articles.body:
Islanders are still struggling to get credit cards despite personal data changes to make it easier to apply for one, a consumer council has said.

The changes which came into force on 30 July meant the government could securely share personal data with UK credit reference agencies, which had been seen as the main barrier to successful applications .

However, the Jersey Consumer Council said several providers had still refused applications and called for the government to work closer with businesses and banks.

A spokesperson for Jersey's government said it had "engaged with providers throughout this process" and whether products were offered in the island "remains a commercial decision".

Carl Walker, from Jersey Consumer Council, said credit card companies would need to be reminded of the change which had allowed more information to be shared.

"The last time they were involved... Jersey was slamming the door shut, so they have switched off and turned their attention elsewhere," he said.

"We're pushing the government to write them an official letter to say this piece of legislation has now changed, Jersey's now open for business... and then leave it up to them whether they decide they to come back or not."

A spokesperson said the government had "successfully delivered a project to share islanders' data with credit reference agencies".

"This was a key issue identified by the industry as an obstacle to providing credit cards in Jersey," they said.

"It remains a commercial decision for providers to decide whether to offer their products or services, including credit cards, in Jersey.

"The government has engaged with providers throughout this process... and will continue to do so."

articles.title: Logos Hope: World's 'largest floating book fair' docks in Belfast
articles.summary: The boat, which has a collection of over 5,000 titles, last visited Belfast in 2009.
articles.body:
An internationally-crewed ship described as the world's "largest floating book fair" has berthed in Belfast.

The Logos Hope is a volunteer-run vessel with a Christian ethos and a bookshop of more than 5,000 titles.

It was officially opened to people in Northern Ireland on Friday by Belfast Lord Mayor Róis-Máire Donelly and will remain open to the public at Albert Quay until 20 October.

Doron Lukat, the managing director of the ship, said Belfast was "one of the first" places the crew aim to visit when travelling to the UK and Europe.

Hannah Gowdy is from Castlederg in County Tyrone and works for the Christian organisation behind the vessel, GBA Ships.

She said she first visited one of the ships in Londonderry in 2004, and described helping bring the Logos Hope back to Northern Ireland as "incredible".

"When I first came to one of the ships, I never imagined being on board and serving as a crew member and then a staff member," she said.

"I think it is an opportunity to help unite Northern Ireland, as well as being able to reconnect with people from here who've served on board."

It is a sentiment that Lukat agrees with.

"We have long-lasting friendships with individuals, institutions and local authorities" in Northern Ireland, he said.

"Over the years, many people from Northern Ireland have volunteered on the ships themselves too.

"So a community has been built up over time of people who support this ministry."

Lukat said he exptected the Logos Hope to have a positive effect locally too.

"Our tagline is sharing knowledge, help and hope," he said.

"I want people to come on board, browse the books, engage with our crew and events, and go back to their communities choosing to be people of hope, coming together rather than dividing."

Education Minister Paul Givan said he was "delighted" to have the boat back in Belfast.

"It is something that I think will bring real excitement," said Givan.

"I hope many people will visit and experience one of the biggest bookstores that you would be able to find, which is important for me as education minister when it comes to literacy.

"The boat is also about bringing a message of hope not just to Belfast but right across the world."

articles.title: Irish budget: Help with energy and childcare costs, while income tax threshold goes up
articles.summary: The threshold at which people start paying the higher income tax rate is also expected to increase.
articles.body:
The Irish government is expected to announce measures to help with energy and childcare costs when it delivers its budget later.

The threshold at which people start paying the higher rate of income tax is also expected to be increased from its current level of €44,000 (£37,000).

The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said the budget has to be about "trying to ease the pressure on families and households".

The broad shape of the budget was set out in the Summer Economic Statement , promising tax measures worth €1.5bn (£1.27bn) and extra spending of €7bn (£5.92bn).

Much of that additional spending is "standstill" funding to cover the rising costs of current services.

Ireland is in a stronger fiscal position than most European countries as an ongoing corporation tax windfall means it is collecting more in taxes than it is spending on services.

Figures released last week showed the country is expected to run a surplus of €6.9bn (£5.84bn) this year, lower than the €9.2bn (£7.79bn) forecast in April.

That smaller forecast surplus reflects the introduction of fuel supports and additional spending to cover budget overspends, particularly in health.

Some of the surplus is being invested in national wealth funds to help with future spending commitments.

A spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, has criticised the government for not saving more.

Other measures expected to be announced on Tuesday are a new tax-free savings scheme, similar to the UK ISA.

A proposal for a "culture card" for teenagers, to spend on events like concerts, is also set to be announced though the value and eligibility are unclear.

Irish government to divert billions of extra euros to savings funds

articles.title: UK oil refinery broke toxic pollution limits dozens of times
articles.summary: Pollution was spilled into local rivers and protected sites, documents shared with the BBC suggest.
articles.body:
One of the UK's biggest oil refineries spilled pollution into local rivers and the Mersey Estuary on dozens of occasions in 2023 and 2024, documents shared exclusively with the BBC suggest.

EET Fuels, formerly known as Essar, which runs Stanlow refinery, pleaded guilty this year to 12 charges of breaching environmental law between 2018 and 2020.

But documents obtained by investigative journalists from SourceMaterial describe other breaches from the refinery in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, with toxic chemicals and oil regularly spilled into the waterways and even groundwater.

EET Fuels said it "takes its environmental responsibilities extremely seriously".

The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed that it is investigating the breaches.

The Stanlow oil refinery is one of only four remaining refineries in the UK and processes 10 million tonnes of crude oil each year - producing around 18% of the country's fuel for road transport like cars and trucks.

EET Fuels, which bought the refinery from Shell in 2011 for £842m , holds a permit to operate the site.

This says it can discharge controlled amounts of oil and chemicals into the air and waterways. However, it must make efforts to limit pollution to the environment and harm to humans.

But reports from the EA into activities at the refinery, uncovered by environmental journalists SourceMaterial, show that in 2023 and 2024 the permitted levels for chemical releases were exceeded hundreds of times.

The regulator has determined this meant EET Fuels broke its permit conditions 58 times over the two-year period - which could amount to an illegal offence.

The documents show the spills included toxic chemicals such as cyanide, benzene, and heavy oils - into the air and local waterways like Thornton Brook and the River Gowy which connect onto the River Mersey Estuary.

The Estuary is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and home to endangered species including dolphins and a breeding ground for rare birds.

"Species like dunlin, blacktail, godwit and red shank will travel all around the world to feed and roost in the land around the River Mersey," explained Charlotte Harris, chief executive of Cheshire Wildlife Trust.

Harris said this has only been possible because organisations, including the Wildlife Trusts, have undertaken years of pollution clean up from legacy industry in the area.

"We've seen the Atlantic salmon return to the river and also the critically endangered European eel makes its way up the Mersey and into the River Gowy to breed each year as well," she said.

EA documents detail how pollutants like sulphur dioxide were released into the air at seven times permitted levels, cyanide into waterways like the Gowy at more than eight times permitted levels, and oil at more than thirteen times the allowed levels.

In one incident in July 2023, the company breached its permit after rainwater containing oil leaked from the site - the EA classed the event as "significant".

In its report it said there were a "significant number" of complaints from locals about the smell and further investigations indicated the oil had contaminated groundwater supplies.

EET Fuels told the BBC that the oil lost was on a "low scale" and "was strictly localised to two boreholes, all well within the Stanlow site itself".

A year later on 12 September 2024, another EA report says that oil was spilled again from the site. Over a 36-hour period more than a tonne of oil was released into Thornton Brook and spread to the Mersey Estuary.

EET Fuels reported the incident to the authorities, but it took nearly two weeks for the company to provide an estimate of how much oil was spilled - another breach of the regulations which requires this within 24 hours.

An emergency response team was organised including regulators the EA and Natural England, local port authorities and the Fisheries Authority - according to meeting documents.

Natural England (NE), which regulates SSSIs, said in one meeting: "What has gone in there is going to have some impact on the vegetation and salt marsh and there is probably still a risk of ingestion by birds."

A drone was sent up to survey the scale of the damage which revealed oil had spread for more than a mile down the river and "there was brown discolouration around the reedbed". The footage showed wading birds - including the red-listed Dunlin - in the area.

"Where we have chemical pollution the impact isn't just localised. When it enters the river system, that system is highly dynamic and high energy, which means that pollution spreads far and wide really, really quickly," said Harris.

A floating barrier was deployed to try and contain the spill.

The regulators decided that because the site was not easily reachable, the public health risk was low, but a decision was made to close local cockle beds in the Estuary while the water quality was tested by the Food Standards Agency (FSA).

The beds were given the all clear, but were closed for five weeks whilst testing took place.

Mark Taylor, CEO of the Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority North West, told the BBC: "The incident led to a delay in the fishers being able to derive an income from the bed".

He added that they were able to make up this income later in the season.

The incident was later categorised by the EA as a "minor" breach of the company's permit.

EET Fuels told the BBC in a statement: "Selectively chosen, historical permit exceedances from prior years in no way represent the current operational status, improving environmental performance, or governance of the refinery today."

The Environment Agency has launched a separate criminal investigation into what happened in September 2024 and told the BBC it remained "ongoing".

It said it was yet to confirm what action to take in relation to the 2023 offences.

As well as the Environment Agency's investigation, Natural England began its own investigation after the 2024 incident.

It eventually dropped this, and told the BBC: "Our assessment found that, while it was regrettable that the incident occurred, the environmental impact on the SSSI was minor."

But in internal emails Natural England told the EA its reason for dropping the investigation was it thought the company's permit to operate did not set any limits for how much oil could be released - despite the pollution risks.

Its officers wrote: "Thank you for sending the permit…. which verify Stanlow's stance that the storm overflow is permitted and further with no limit set to the quantity of oil released. With this in place, Natural England have decided not to take any further action."

James Wallace, chief executive at charity River Action, said these documents suggest "we're seeing a downgrading of pollution incident[s]... where evidence is being ignored."

When asked about its reasons for dropping the investigation, Natural England said its role was to assess the impact on the protected site and that any questions about "compliance with the environmental permit are matters for the Environment Agency".

EET Fuels is due to be sentenced next month for the previous permit breaches between 2018 and 2020.

Wallace said the fact this case took up to eight years to reach the courts and the company appears to have breached environmental law repeatedly, calls into question the effectiveness of the regulators in deterring environmental pollution.

"We need to see consistent law enforcement, and we need to see the threat of punitive measures by all industries, whether it's the water industry or oil refineries," Wallace said.

Harris from Cheshire Wildlife Trust agreed the current regulations were "not solving the problem at source at the moment".

"So when a business does impact a river like this, it is absolutely vital that they're held to account. But going further than that, it shouldn't be happening in the first place. We really do need to get a grip of how we treat our river systems," she added.

EET Fuels, also told the BBC: "[It] has backed its environmental commitments with decisive action, investing over £24 million in major wastewater infrastructure alone and delivering a measurable, upward trend in Environment Agency compliance ratings, improving from an F rating in 2023 to an E rating in 2024 as major capital projects came online."

images.caption: Stanlow oil refinery in Cheshire is the second largest in the UK
